item.title: [Sports Illustrated] MLB’s 2026 Photo of the Year Belongs to Brewers' William Contreras
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown

item.content:encoded:
If there is one photo that is going to sum up the 2026 Major League Baseball season, it is going to be the shot of Milwaukee Brewers star William Contreras right after the World Series came to a close on Wednesday night.
This photo was a long time coming. It took 57 years for the Brewers organization to hoist a World Series trophy for the first time. This image of Contreras, who was named as the 2026 World Series Most Valuable Player, is a perfect representation of the pure bliss and elation that the fanbase and organization felt on Wednesday night.
Game 5 Was Baseball At It's Best
Baseball brings people together. Whether you're a fan of the Brewers, or any other team in the league, history was made on Wednesday night and fans were paying attention. This is what the league can be when it's at its best. Two great teams faced off in the World Series in the Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays and it just so happened that it was the Brewers came out on top. Fans got to witness a great series and saw two teams playing the right way. In this case, the Brewers won their first title and we came away with this photo. If the Rays had won, it would've been their first title as well.
All in all, a great season ended on a high note.
Unfortunately, now we have to wait until March, at the very least, for real, meaningful games to begin again. But that's not even a guarantee. The collective bargaining agreement will expire in December and there's no way to know right now when the two sides will sort out the labor issues facing the league. The league wants a salary cap and the MLBPA does not. That's going to be at the crux of the discussion this winter, although there's far more than just that simplified summary.
Neither side has come close to caving yet, which isn't shocking. The two sides are negotiating and neither side has a reason to give in yet. But it would be a mistake if they don't meet in the middle and find a way to not ruin the momentum the league has right now. Viewership was up around the league all year and fans were just rewarded with an elite postseason. The baseball world is paying attention. Game 5 on Wednesday night was a perfect example of baseball at its best. Hopefully, the offseason isn't at its worst.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick also received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Fastball On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.content:encoded:
Christian Yelich Dedicates Brewers’ First World Series Title To Bob Uecker
Christian Yelich has waited a long time to call himself a World Series champion.
In the middle of the celebration, his thoughts turned to the man who wanted it as badly as anyone.
After the Milwaukee Brewers beat the Tampa Bay Rays 4-1 in Game 5 to clinch the first championship in franchise history, Yelich spoke with FOX Sports’ Ken Rosenthal. Rosenthal asked what longtime Brewers broadcaster Bob Uecker would be thinking if he were looking down.
"He’s smiling, man. He’s smiling," Yelich said. "I really wish he could have been here to see this. … But like we said a bunch, he’s been with us a lot. We keep him close to our hearts. And this one’s still for Bob."
Bob Uecker, who died in 2025, was the longtime voice of the Brewers. (Photo by John Fisher/Getty Images)
Uecker, the voice of the Brewers for 54 seasons, died in January 2025 at 90 from small-cell lung cancer, months after calling his final Brewers postseason game. His diagnosis was never made public, but those closest to him knew, including Yelich.
During the Stand Up To Cancer moment in Game 4, every Brewers player’s placard read "UECK." (Photo by Mary DeCicco/MLB Photos via Getty Images)
Uecker’s memory followed the Brewers throughout October.
During Game 4 on Tuesday, play paused after the fifth inning for the annual Stand Up To Cancer moment, when everyone in the ballpark holds up a placard with the name of someone affected by cancer.
As cameras panned across the Brewers lined up in front of their dugout, every placard carried the same name: "UECK."
"It just feels like it’s fitting, the obvious choice to make," Yelich said afterwards.
Yelich has seen this Brewers run take shape since the day he arrived in Milwaukee.
Acquired from the Miami Marlins in January 2018, he won NL MVP in his first season in Milwaukee.
He’s now the second-longest-tenured Brewer behind Brandon Woodruff, and they’re the last two players left from the 2018 team that lost Game 7 of the NLCS to the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Eight years later, Milwaukee finally finished the job. The Brewers swept the Dodgers in the NLCS and then beat the Rays to bring home the city’s first World Series title.
"We’re coming home, baby," Yelich told Rosenthal when asked for his message to Brewers fans. "We can’t wait to see you. Can’t wait to celebrate."

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Cam Schlittler Named AL Outstanding Pitcher by His Fellow MLB Players
item.dc:creator: Chris Trant
item.description: The New York Yankees put together a strong regular season during the 2026 MLB season, finishing 93-68 and earning the top American League Wild Card spot before sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the opening round of the postseason. However, their postseason run came to a screeching halt in the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays. The Yankees were swept by the Rays, who would eventually go on to win the American League Pennant. While New York's season ended in disappointment, one of the biggest positives
item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees put together a strong regular season during the 2026 MLB season, finishing 93-68 and earning the top American League Wild Card spot before sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the opening round of the postseason.
However, their postseason run came to a screeching halt in the ALDS against the Tampa Bay Rays. The Yankees were swept by the Rays, who would eventually go on to win the American League Pennant. While New York's season ended in disappointment, one of the biggest positives from the year was the emergence of right-hander Cam Schlittler in his second MLB season.
Schlittler started 33 games for the Yankees this season, going 14-6 and posting an American League-leading 1.95 ERA, with 239 strikeouts and a 0.92 WHIP over 193.2 innings. Schlittler was one of the most dominant pitchers in the American League this season and is a heavy favorite to win the AL Cy Young Award for 2026.
While Schlittler will have to wait until Nov. 11 for the Cy Young voting results, the Yankees announced on Wednesday that the right-hander was named the 2026 Players Choice Awards AL Outstanding Pitcher.
Presented by the MLB Players Association, the award is voted on by active players across the league. Schlittler was among three finalists, including Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and Sonny Gray of the Boston Red Sox.
After showing promise as a rookie in 2025, the 25-year-old made a significant leap in his second year and earned his first career All-Star selection.
Schlittler also carried his regular season success into the postseason, where he pitched 6⅓ scoreless innings, striking out 10 in Game 1 of the Wild Card series against the Red Sox.
With the Players Choice Award now added to his résumé, Schlittler has quickly become one of the most accomplished young pitchers in baseball.
Greatest Yankees of All-Time

item.content:encoded:
The Toronto Blue Jays' first season after losing Bo Bichette in free agency to the New York Mets wasn't a good one.
A year after Bichette helped the Blue Jays reach Game 7 of the World Series, this team missed the postseason entirely. Technically, they held onto mathematical hope until the final week of the season, but Toronto was sledding uphill for most of the season.
Bichette's season with the Mets didn't go much better. He took a big step back from his 2025 performance, and New York was even further out of the playoff picture than the Blue Jays.
It all sets up for a fascinating offseason, because Bichette's three-year, $126 million deal with the Mets actually has an opt-out built in after each season. If he wants to be a free agent again this offseason, Bichette can be.
That doesn't mean the Blue Jays would bring him back, but it does mean Bichette's next steps are still to be determined. He's not guaranteed to play with the Mets in 2027. He's got a decision to make.
And there's some new intel on what Bichette might do.
Bo Bichette Update
SNY's Chelsea Janes, a plugged-in MLB insider, put out a mailbag article on Wednesday in which she was asked what she thinks Bichette might do.
Janes' short answer was that she thinks Bichette will opt-in and stay on his current contract with the Mets. But she had plenty more to say and explain.
"My read – and it is truly just my read, because no one has said anything to me definitively – is that Bichette will opt in," Janes writes. "I say that for a few reasons, one of which is as simple as he did not look like a player saying his goodbyes when he left Washington on the last day of the season. Plus, that day, both Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor spoke like they expected to have him back more than simply hoped for it. But reading into things like that is risky and certainly is not enough to say anything for sure."
It also seems that even though Bichette and the Mets didn't have a good year, they liked their time together.
"The other evidence I have is that people around the Mets – so people who spend time around the team daily but are not necessarily in decision-making capacities to know first-hand – also seem fairly convinced Bichette will stay," Janes writes. "He has spoken glowingly of Andy Green. He seems to want to prove he can succeed in New York. And frankly, he isn't going to get anywhere near the average annual value on another deal they gave him on this one. He seemed to settle into the clubhouse down the stretch, much like everyone did. So read into that what you will."
That line about the money that Janes throws in there is probably the most relevant piece here, too.
Bo Bichette Salary
If Bichette stays on his current deal, he'd make $42 million in the 2027 season.
Opting-out does include a $5 million buyout (which accounts for two season and $84 million remaining), so Bichette would still have to get about $40 million per year on a new free agent deal to make it financially logical to opt-out.
If he really didn't like the Mets, Bichette could still choose to leave and start anew elsewhere.
But a year after leaving the Blue Jays, it's currently looking unlikely that Bichette would leave his next team this quickly.
This article was originally published on HEAVY
The post Blue Jays Learn Bo Bichette's Likely MLB Future appeared first on HEAVY.

Josh Inglis' expert pick: Jacob Misiorowski Under 15.5 outs
Price: 53¢ at Polymarket
I have this priced at 60%, and the odds are already dropping. The Tampa Bay Rays have seen Jacob Misiorowski once, and the 24-year-old might be running on fumes. He's thrown 13 1/3 postseason innings on top of 174 2/3 during the regular season after logging just 130 frames in 2025.
He's been laboring through his playoff starts and threw just 78 pitches in Game 1 of the World Series. He hasn't recorded more than 15 outs in any of his three postseason starts, and the familiarity edge now shifts toward Tampa.
Even with a good outing, I see five innings as his ceiling. At 53%, there's still value in backing the Under.
Joe Osborne's expert pick: Brewers moneyline
Price: 57¢ at Polymarket
The Milwaukee Brewers are 12-0 in Misiorowski’s last 12 starts and 23-4 since May 1.
Milwaukee also owns the bullpen edge this World Series: a 1.29 ERA compared to Tampa Bay’s 4.12, and another reliever-heavy night looms for the Rays after using six pitchers in Game 3 and seven in Game 4.
At the plate, Milwaukee’s .773 series OPS dwarfs Tampa’s atrocious .491.
With an elite starter, a stronger bullpen, and a more productive lineup, I’m backing the Brewers to finish the job tonight
Neil Parker's expert pick: William Contreras Over 1.5 hits + runs + RBI
Price: 51¢ at Polymarket
Even with a 0-for-5 night at the dish in Game 4, Milwaukee catcher William Contreras has gone 7-for-17 with a run and three RBI during the World Series.
He’s sporting a .454 wOBA for the postseason while hitting in the heart of the lineup, so I recommend this Over up to 55%. Contreras posted a nearly identical .760 OPS against left-handed pitchers and .756 OPS against righties during the regular season, too
Dustin Saracini's expert pick: Chandler Simpson Over 1.5 hits + runs + RBI
Price: 44¢ at Polymarket
I'd play this up to 48%.
Chandler Simpson has been one of the Rays' most reliable bats throughout the World Series. He's recorded at least one hit in five of his last six postseason games, highlighted by a three-hit performance in Game 4.
He played a pivotal role in Tampa's two-run comeback in the 12th inning, continuing to deliver the goods for a team that's largely been counted out.
He's 3-for-5 against the Miz in his career, and at this price, you have to make that trade

item.content:encoded:
The MLB World Series is finally here after several weeks of intense playoff action. The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time in 44 years. The Rays beat out the Guardians in six games to win the American League pennant for just the third time. Just like in this year's WNBA Finals, we're about to witness history: Whoever wins, this will be the franchise's first championship.
The Milwaukee Brewers are currently in the lead with three wins; they only need one more to win the entire World Series. But it's still anyone's game. Which team will come out on top? Here's how you can watch tonight's World Series game live, even for free.
What Time Is the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays Game?
Game 5 of the World Series between the Rays and Brewers will take place on Wednesday, October 28, at 8:00 p.m. ET.
How to Watch the Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays?
This year, the World Series will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One app. You can also watch it with a live TV or sports streaming subscription from DirecTV, Fubo, Hulu, Sling, Sportsnet+ (if you're in Canada), or YouTube TV.
How to Watch the Brewers vs. Rays for Free
If you don't want to subscribe to any of the above platforms, you may be able to sign up for a few free trials to gain access to the remaining games. Fox One and Hulu offer three-day trials, DirecTV and Fubo offer five days, and YouTube TV gives you 10 days for free.
2026 MLB World Series Game Schedule
MLB's expanded postseason means more teams on the playoff schedule. In the Wild Card round, the Braves beat the Phillies, the Padres beat the Cubs, the Yankees defeated the Red Sox, and the White Sox defeated the Astros. The winners advanced to the Division Series, where the Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays, and Cleveland Guardians beat their respective opponents.
For the Championship Series, the Brewers beat the Dodgers in four games to clinch the National League pennant. The Rays defeated the Guardians in six games to capture the American League pennant. Now, Milwaukee and Tampa Bay will face off in the best-of-seven World Series to begin on October 23. Who will get to raise the trophy?
World Series: Milwaukee Brewers vs. Tampa Bay Rays - MIL leads 3-1
- Game 5 on October 28 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 6 on October 30 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 7 on October 31 - Fox/Fox One*
*if necessary
How to Stream the 2026 MLB Playoffs
This year's MLB postseason is stretched across multiple networks and streaming services. All Wild Card Series games for the American League and National League were broadcast on NBC, NBCSN, and Peacock. ALDS and ALCS games were on TBS/TruTV and HBO Max, while NLDS and NLCS games were on Fox/FS1. For the World Series, all games will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One streaming service.
- DirecTV: DirecTV's MySports base pack costs $45 per month for the first six months to see every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, and TBS/TruTV.
- Fox One: Fox's own streaming app lets you watch the NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox and FS1 for $20 per month.
- Fubo: Fubo's Sports plan costs $45.99 for the first month to watch the Wild Card Series, NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox, FS1, and NBC/NBCSN.
- HBO Max: If you pay for the $18.49-per-month HBO Max Standard, you'll be able to watch the ALDS and ALCS games on TBS/TruTV.
- Hulu: For $90 per month, you can watch every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, TBS, and TruTV.
- Peacock: Instead of a live TV service, you'd need to pay $10.99 per month for Peacock Premium to see the Wild Card Series games.
- Sling: The $60.99-per-month Sling Orange & Blue bundle will let you watch the ALDS and ALCS on TBS/TruTV and the NLDS and NLCS on FS1. Day Passes are also available for Sling Orange, allowing you to watch games on TBS for up to seven days.
- Sportsnet+ (Canada only): The $30-per-month Standard tier lets you watch every postseason game.
- YouTube TV: Though the standard plan for YouTube TV costs $83 per month, you can actually now pay for the cheaper $65 Sports package to see all games on Fox, FS1, NBC/NBCSN, and TBS/TruTV.
Can I Watch Postseason Games on MLB.TV?
Are you already an MLB.TV subscriber? You can watch the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series games through MLB's own streaming service—but there's a catch. To watch on MLB.TV, you'll first need to authenticate through a participating pay TV provider. It's such a sticking point that it makes the entire question moot. If you already have a TV provider, then you wouldn't need to use a streaming service. If you don't already have an MLB.TV subscription, don't pay for one now.
How can I listen to the 2026 postseason?
You can also listen to the games via ESPN Radio.
Which Teams Are In the Playoffs?
Since MLB expanded its postseason picture in 2022, a total of 12 teams make the playoffs each year. That includes six teams per league, including the three division winners and three Wild Card teams.
- American League Division Winners: Tampa Bay Rays (1), Cleveland Guardians (2), Houston Astros (3)
- American League Wild Card: New York Yankees (4), Boston Red Sox (5), Chicago White Sox (6)
- National League Division Winners: Milwaukee Brewers (1), Los Angeles Dodgers (2), Atlanta Braves (3)
- National League Wild Card: Chicago Cubs (4), Philadelphia Phillies (5), San Diego Padres (6)
Upgrade Your Streaming Experience
If you decide to watch the MLB postseason, there's still time to get a big-screen television for viewing this beautiful game. Pro tip: Turn on your TV's motion-smoothing option for the best picture while watching sports. Just remember to turn it off before watching other TV shows and movies to avoid the awful "soap opera" effect.
About Our Expert
As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert.
I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week.
My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth.
My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work.
Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — With some pent-up energy and a fearless attitude, the Tampa Bay Rays extended their season at least one more day and will play host to Game 5 of the World Series on Wednesday.
With the Rays down to their last three outs, Jonny DeLuca and Ben Williamson provided the heroics to alter the narrative after Tampa Bay had been stymied at every turn over the first three games by the Milwaukee Brewers.
After falling into a 3-0 series hole, the Rays will now try to lean into their new-found momentum, but first they need to come up with a pitching plan.
Tampa Bay right-hander Nick Martinez would have been the probable Game 5 starter, but he was needed to pitch two innings on Tuesday.
“We’re going to get together after this session and sit down and talk about pitching,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said after the victory. “Going to check who’s available. I’m going to guess most guys are going to say they’re capable of an inning or more given it’s Game 5 of the World Series, but nothing has been decided yet.”
The Brewers tied the Tuesday game 2-2 in the fifth inning on a home run from David Hamilton, and the score remained even until the 12th when Cooper Pratt hit a home run for Milwaukee.
Down 3-2, Tampa Bay caught a rare break when Brewers third baseman Joey Ortiz committed a throwing error on Junior Caminero’s grounder to open the bottom of the 12th. Liam Hicks singled before DeLuca delivered an RBI single to center to tie the game 3-all.
After a Chandler Simpson single loaded the bases with no outs, Williamson came on to pinch-hit and bounced a ball into right field to set off a Rays celebration on the infield.
“Cash just kind of turned around and said, ‘Get ready to hit,'” Williamson said. “Jokingly in my head, I was thinking, ‘Yeah, I’ve been ready to hit since the fourth or fifth inning.'”
The Brewers now have one more opportunity to clinch their first-ever World Series title on the road, then would play host to Games 6 and 7, if necessary.
“Nobody said any of this was going to be easy, but I think we have the right group to get a good night’s sleep, flush it and be ready to go (Wednesday),” said Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers, who is 2-for-17 with three walks in the series after winning the National League Championship Series MVP award.
While Tampa Bay scrambles to put together a pitching plan, Milwaukee will send NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski to the mound. The hard-throwing right-hander allowed one run over five innings to earn the win in Game 1.
In three starts and 13 1/3 innings this postseason, Misiorowski is 1-0 with a 2.70 ERA and 14 strikeouts, although he had just three against the Rays in the series opener.
“You can write it up and hope that they perform like the back of their baseball card, but that doesn’t always happen,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said after announcing Misiorowski as his starter. “You go with what you believe is the deal. I trust our guys. They put themselves in a position to win.”
While the Rays used seven pitchers to keep their season alive in Game 4, the Brewers went even deeper by using eight in an unsuccessful attempt to close out their first-ever World Series championship. Game 5 could come down to which bullpen bounces back best.
“You’re seeing two elite contact offenses where strikeouts are very tough to come by,” Cash said. “We weren’t knocking balls in the gap or knocking balls out of the ballpark. We pieced together a big (12th inning), maybe the most important inning of our season.”
–Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Game 4 of the World Series between the Milwaukee Brewers and Tampa Bay Rays begins at 8:00 p.m. ET on Tuesday, October 27, televised by FOX. The Brewers are favored with a 1.75x payout to win on PrizePicks.
The Milwaukee Brewers lead 3-0 in the World Series after routing the Tampa Bay Rays 10-1 in Game 3 on Monday. Milwaukee is now one win away from securing the franchise's first World Series championship, while Tampa Bay faces elimination and must win four consecutive games to complete an improbable comeback.
The Rays will turn to SP Griffin Jax in Game 4, hoping the right-hander can slow down a Brewers lineup that has dominated the World Series. Milwaukee has not announced its starting pitcher, potentially setting up another bullpen game as the club looks to complete the sweep.
Below, we'll break down our Brewers vs. Rays prediction and picks for Tuesday's World Series Game 4, including the winner and player picks for PrizePicks.
{{mlb_offer_banner="/style-system/ui-components-playbook"}}
Brewers vs. Rays Prediction, Winner Payout, Over/Under for World Series Game 4
Milwaukee enters Game 4 as the road favorite, returning a 1.75x payout if it wins outright.
Here are the full payouts for the Brewers vs. Rays game. PrizePicks data is live at the time of writing and is subject to change.
Make your Brewers vs. Rays prediction on the winner on PrizePicks.
Unless otherwise noted, data used in this article is from FanGraphs, Baseball Savant, and MLB.com.
Griffin Jax (3.41 xFIP) will take the ball for Tampa Bay as the Rays' season hangs in the balance. The right-hander finished the regular season 8-10 with a 3.53 ERA and 116 strikeouts.
He faces a tough assignment against a Milwaukee offense that has consistently put runners on base throughout the World Series, but his regular-season home success could help him tonight.
Jax has struggled during the postseason, allowing 4 earned runs over six innings in his previous playoff appearances.
We can talk all we want about Tampa’s pitching plans, but ultimately the Rays offense will need a much better showing against Milwaukee's pitching staff if they want to save their season.
Despite being so good at getting runners on base and capitalizing with runners in scoring position during the regular season, the Rays managed just 1 run and struggled to generate sustained offense in Game 3. Those same issues plagued Tampa Bay in the first two games of this series.
The Brewers' pitching plans remain uncertain heading into tonight. Milwaukee has not announced a starter, and a bullpen-heavy approach seems most likely with the championship within reach.
The Brewers used LHP Robert Gasser in Game 3, and he delivered one of the postseason's most dominant starts, allowing just 1 hit over six innings while striking out 6.
Gasser's performance gave Milwaukee's bullpen valuable rest, which could prove significant if the Brewers need multiple relievers to get through Game 4. Milwaukee's pitching staff has been outstanding throughout the postseason, allowing just 7 runs across its first three World Series games.
The Brewers offense has stolen the show this World Series. At one point last night, they recorded eight straight two-out hits to blow the game wide open — a truly magnificent team feat on the grandest stage of all.

item.dc:creator: Dibyendu Mondal

Kirk and his wife, Sofia Castañeda, went to cheer on his childhood best friend, Tampa Bay Rays first baseman Jonathan Aranda. Castañeda shared the moment on Instagram. Jonathan Aranda’s Dad Sends Touching Message About Alejandro Kirk H
item.content:encoded:
Toronto Blue Jays catcher Alejandro Kirk attended Game 3 of the World Series on Monday night at Tropicana Field.
Kirk and his wife, Sofia Castañeda, went to cheer on his childhood best friend, Tampa Bay Rays first baseman Jonathan Aranda. Castañeda shared the moment on Instagram.
It was the second straight round in which Kirk watched Aranda in person. Aranda’s father also spoke about the two friends and their long road together.
Jonathan Aranda’s Dad Sends Touching Message About Alejandro Kirk
Humberto Aranda, Jonathan’s father, attended Game 3 as well. He spoke with Mexican media about his son and Kirk during the World Series.
“Definitely seeing Alejandro, seeing Jonathan, seeing them here after so many years of following them… they played together, they started playing together at the age of three and this path that they are still following together is completely rewarding,” he said. “And for the families, for both families, the journey has been very good, very beautiful, and we are very happy to be able to live the experience.”
Humberto was an assistant coach on the boys’ Little League team in Tijuana, Mexico. Kirk’s father, Juan Manuel Kirk, managed that team.
Kirk and Aranda have been friends since they were 3. They played on the same youth teams for 12 years. They still work out at the same gym in Tijuana.
The friends traded places this fall. Last October, Aranda watched from the stands as Kirk played in the World Series. He wore a jersey from their old Tijuana youth team, the Glu-Glu, with a World Series patch.
When Kirk homered in Game 1, Aranda started a social media campaign to recover the ball. “It was a big thing for me to go see him,” Aranda said during the ALCS.
Now Kirk is returning the favor.
Alejandro Kirk Also Watched Aranda Clinch the Pennant at Tropicana Field
Monday was not Kirk’s first trip to Tropicana Field this postseason. He attended Game 6 of the American League Championship Series on Oct. 19.
Kirk has been keeping up with games at Tropicana Field. He has been in the area for work. He has been training at the Blue Jays’ player development complex in Dunedin, Florida.
Kirk was spotted at the complex on Oct. 23, getting an early start on the 2027 season. The current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1. A lockout after that date would bar players on 40-man rosters from team facilities.

This could be the final MLB game for quite some time as the Milwaukee Brewers have a chance to sweep the Tampa Bay Rays in the 2026 World Series on Tuesday night.
Milwaukee scored eight runs with two outs in the fifth inning in Game 3 last night, putting up 10 runs without a home run in the 10-1 victory.
There have now been just two home runs through three games in this series, both of which came in Game 2.
Nevertheless, I have a home run pick for each team in World Series Game 4 tonight.
Here’s a complete breakdown of these home run props for Tuesday, Oct. 27.
Best MLB Home Run Prop Bet Picks for Tuesday, Oct. 27.
- Yandy Diaz to Hit a Home Run (+800)
- William Contreras to Hit a Home Run (+540)
Yandy Diaz to Hit a Home Run (+800)
There weren’t any home runs in Game 3, but Yandy Diaz came pretty darn close. His 413-foot double with an exit velocity of 111.4 miles per hour would’ve been a home run in 22 of 30 ballparks, according to Baseball Savant. He also had a single with an exit velocity of 115.5 miles per hour.
Diaz had 22 home runs in the regular season and went deep twice in the ALCS. I’ll take this long +800 price given the power he has and how well he’s seeing the ball right now.
William Contreras to Hit a Home Run (+540)
I am going down with the ship.
After hitting 18 home runs in the regular season, Contreras has gone deep three times this postseason. The last one came in NLCS Game 2, the start of a six-game hitting streak for the slugger.
Contreras is now 18-for-43 (.419) with three home runs and a double in 11 postseason games. He’s racked up eight RBI and six runs as well.

item.title: [North Side Baseball] How Alex Bregman's Arrival Brought Dansby Swanson Back to the Shortstop Upper Crust—For Now
item.dc:creator: Matthew Trueblood
item.description: Cubs Video What Alex Bregman can do on the field—the statistical contribution he can make when it's his turn to bat and when the ball is hit his way—is plenty valuable. item.content:encoded:
Cubs Video
What Alex Bregman can do on the field—the statistical contribution he can make when it's his turn to bat and when the ball is hit his way—is plenty valuable. By the end of the 2026 season, that was obvious. Bregman was one of the best hitters in baseball from mid-July onward, and he won the Fielding Bible Award at third base for his supernal defense. Multiple teams were willing to give him a fat five-year deal last offseason, and most of that money is for the way he hits and fields.
However, Bregman also has enormous value as a facilitator, a leader, and an organization changer. That's what made the Cubs willing to outbid the Red Sox and others for his services; it was the extra cushion they needed to feel safe spashing so much money on a player who would turn 32 just days after playing his first regular-season game for them. In those areas, he was arguably an even greater success in 2026 than on the stat sheet. The partnership of Bregman and Pete Crow-Armstrong, offensively, was about more than the fact that they hit back-to-back at the top of the lineup 24 times. They made improvements that followed the same patterns. They communicated about what they were seeing from each opposing pitcher. Bregman thrived down the stretch, but his input also helped Crow-Armstrong break the game, even while the veteran was still mired in a long early funk.
Defensively, his partnership would be with shortstop Dansby Swanson. Bregman replaced Swanson as the highest-paid player on the team and as the team's resident emblem of intention to win and dedication to whatever that takes. Swanson was the first overall pick in 2015; Bregman was the second. Swanson won the 2021 World Series with the team from near Atlanta. Bregman won the World Baseball Classic and the Series in 2017, then another Series in 2022. Swanson's championship came at Bregman's expense, too, as his club beat Houston in that Fall Classic. The two players' history was interwoven, and they would need to prove they could achieve as much together as they had (seemingly) working at odds, to top one another.
It couldn't have worked out more beautifully, or in a fashion more quintessentially Bregman. Here's the gist: In 2025, Swanson's defensive numbers dipped. That wasn't surprising. He was 31 years old, which is already getting a bit old for a shortstop in the majors today. He doesn't have an elite arm (or even, in truth, an average one), and though he learned long ago to get rid of the ball exceptionally quickly when needed, that can't make up for everything. He suffered, in particular, on exactly the balls you would expect an aging non-premium athlete to suffer on: ones hit to his right, where he had to range into the hole and make the toughest plays asked of shortstops. According to Baseball Savant, Swanson dropped from 16 and 12 runs saved in 2023 and 2024, respectively, to just 2 in 2025. The biggest difference came on balls that forced him to move toward third base:
- 2023: 8 Outs Above Average
- 2024: 2
- 2025: -1
The Cubs didn't do what many teams might have done in such a situation, though. First of all, they didn't even briefly consider moving Swanson to second base and trading Nico Hoerner. That would have been a viable option; Hoerner was an impending free agent until he signed a six-year extension last spring. The Cubs believed Swanson could still be a great defensive shortstop, though, and that Hoerner's defensive work as his double-play partner was too valuable to lose.
Even with the same personnel in place, though, they could have more aggressively shaded their infield alignments, putting Swanson a step or two closer to the hole when there was a chance he would be called upon to make a play there. Instead, they used fairly traditional setups. The 2025 Cubs were 17th in shading their infield, doing so 53% of the time against left-handed batters and 6% of the time against righties. That led to a lot of plays that looked like this.
Seeing the ball zip past Swanson like that makes him seem slow, but that's unfair. Alec Bohm hit that grounder at 104 miles per hour. To make the play, Swanson needed to be a step farther in the direction he had to go. Failing that, not even a younger, more explosive player would get there. But the even more telling plays, perhaps, were those that looked more like this.
This ball isn't hit so hard, and Swanson has the quick feet to run it down. However, because he started at a neutral position, he had to run an extra step or two before snaring the bounce. That meant throwing off-balance, on the run, which robbed him of the ability to be accurate and powerful. This is where being 31 and a bit less strong-armed than most shortstops caught up to him, but much of the reason was his starting position.
Early in 2026, the same thing was happening too often. Swanson would flag down a ball that seemed ticketed for left field, but because he did so at the very edge of his range, he still couldn't record an out.
Over time, though, a (literal) shift took place. Bregman, who played with one of the game's most aggressive shifting teams in Houston before the league outlawed the true shift, advocated for a bit more proactive shading with his new club. They didn't become an extreme team, but they did become one of the league leaders in that area. In 2026, the Cubs shaded their infield 67% of the time against lefties and 14% of the time against righties, moving them into the top seven in shading, overall. Swanson started making plays that he couldn't make the previous year.
There were balls, like the one above, that would have been clean singles to left field in 2025 but became great plays in 2026. There were also plenty that might have become infield hits in 2025, but which ended up looking routine this year.
Swanson's numbers rebounded, especially on those balls that took him toward third base: he got back to 8 OAA on them. The way OAA tabulates value, that actually took a bite out of Bregman. He rated worse (-6 OAA) on balls to his left than he ever has before. But Bregman didn't care. By playing closer to the line against right-handed batters, he was better able to set himself for long throws when he made a play along the foul line, and he got better coming in on slowly hit balls. He was the best he's ever been at third, precisely because he ceded a bit of range to his superb partner on the left side of the infield.
Communication between those two players is more important than many who watch the game from home might realize. They don't call each other off in quite the same way outfielders do, but there has to be an understanding between the shortstop and the third baseman: when to take a ball and when to let it go; whether your partner will break to cover a base, and how to back them up if they go for the ball instead; where your teammate should throw the ball, if fielding it took him in a direction that makes it hard for him to see the whole diamond. Bregman and Swanson worked gloriously together in their first year as a tandem, which helped the Cubs reach the postseason and provided hope for the short-term aging profile of each.
That doesn't mean it won't get harder. As each moves into his mid-30s, they'll have to continue communicating, adapting and adjusting. Working together is important, but it can't entirely make up for the fact that each individual is getting a bit older, a bit slower and a bit less able to react in the blink of an eye. Next year, the Cubs' infield defense will probably be worse. That's the nature of investing so much in players who would ordinarily move off their positions, and slotting them into a roster that doesn't permit them to do so. What we saw in the first year of Bregman and Swanson, though, is that they're likely to weather those degradations better than most, because of their savvy and their shared commitment to doing whatever it takes to win.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] World Series 2026: Brewers' DH Christian Yelich turns pivotal play of World Series Game 3 with speed and instincts — 'Nobody cares about baserunning more than him'
item.dc:creator: Jake Mintz

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG — The Brewers won by a mile because they're obsessed with the inches.
Nobody would describe the final outcome of Milwaukee's emphatic beatdown on Monday — a 10-1 drubbing of the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the World Series — as "close." Not since 2015 has there been a larger margin of victory in a World Series game. The Brewers' 16-to-3 hit advantage over the flailing Rays was the third-largest in Fall Classic history. Starter Robert Gasser allowed just one one hit and faced the minimum across six brilliant innings, becoming the first lefty to do that in a World Series game since Sandy Koufax in 1965. A massive gathering of Brewers fans, an estimated 30% of the crowd, was there to witness it all, their voices joyously hoarse by the end.
It was a shellacking of historic proportions.
But Milwaukee's commanding 3-0 series lead, one that places this franchise on the precipice of its first championship, was earned in the margins on a bang-bang play that folks in the Badger State will remember for a long time.
Up a pair in the top of the fifth, the Brewers put runners on first and second against Tampa Bay starter Freddy Peralta. Milwaukee catcher William Contreras, the best hitter in these playoffs, ripped a two-hopper toward third baseman Junior Caminero. In a spinning motion, Tampa's talented talisman snagged the pearl and flicked it to second baseman Ben Williamson as a full-bore Christian Yelich slid into the bag. Umpire Dan Bellino punched his fist. The FOX graphic evaporated from the screen. Multiple members of Tampa Bay's between-innings hype squad jogged onto the outfield track for some type of giveaway.
Yelich, though, clung to the bag with his left hand as he motioned adamantly toward Belino with his right.
"Safe, safe."
Safe, indeed.
The Brewers challenged the call. Before Bellino could finish announcing the overturn, Tampa Bay skipper Kevin Cash was already headed toward the mound to pull Peralta.
But no move, at that point, could have stopped the inevitable.
"The whole game was changed when Yeli was safe at second," Brewer manager Pat Murphy insisted afterwards. "That's just a hustle play. When your leader makes that play, that says it all. The game was changed because he did a little thing that anybody can do."
Yelich, by beating the throw to second, turned a dead frame into the inning of a lifetime. The floodgates soon burst, sweeping away Tampa's next pitcher, Cam Booser. On a 2-2 count, he served a mid-zone fastball to second baseman Brice Turang, who scorched one off shortstop Taylor Walls' glove and into the outfield. Milwaukee's lead was doubled.
As the sizable traveling contingent — a bar down the street sold out of Miller Lite before first pitch — went berzerk, the Fox broadcast panned to a young Rays fan, who could be seen uttering to his companion a harsh and humbling realization: "That's the series."
Milwaukee, though, would leave no doubt. And then some.
Their next five batters all found grass, with each consequential hit eliciting louder and louder roars from the armada of traveling Wisconsinites. In total, the Brewers strung together seven consecutive two-out hits to plate eight two-out runs, a World Series record. It was an all-time heater and a fitting performance from a pridefully selfless Brewers offense that has prioritized passing the baton over hitting big flies all season long.
"Nobody wants to be the hero," hitting coach Dan Vogelbach boasted.
That might be true, but Yelich, with his mad dash to second, was the under-the-radar hero of this evening.
With the right-handed Contreras at the plate and a runner on second, Rays first baseman Ryan Villade was shaded toward second, opting not to hold Yelich on. That allowed the Brewers' captain to take a much larger-than-average lead off first base. By the time Contreras swung, Yelich was already about 30 feet from the bag, his right foot in the air ready to break in either direction. As the ball bounced toward Caminero, Yelich landed and broke hard for second.
"You have to understand where you're at in space," Yelich explained postgame. "You're lengthening your primary [lead] in case there's a ball in the hole or some sort of play happens where you could potentially beat the throw."
It was a sublime bit of baserunning, the kind that takes years of purposeful, monotonous practice to get good at. There's also an element of internal pre-pitch preparation: "If X happens, I do Y." Yelich executed that process perfectly. Caminero, who had ample time to get the slow-footed Contreras at first, did not.
"The beauty of it is that you have guys like Yeli that demand it from the group," first-base coach Spencer Allen told Yahoo Sports about the team's attention to detail.
Jason Lane, Milwaukee's offense and strategy coordinator, explained to Yahoo Sports that he tells players to approach a secondary lead at first base and two outs with the same intent and intensity they would bring to a "contact play." That's the inside-baseball term for when a runner at third, with the infield drawn in, plans to race home on contact — no matter where the ball's hit.
"When you remind guys of that and explain it to them like that — and these guys are hunting all those little things that we preach about right turns — it can become something that happens in a playoff game," he explained.
On a team that cares deeply about the little things, Yelich, the group's most accomplished character, might care most of all. That establishes a standard, one that has helped push the Brewers to an amazing 10-1 record this postseason. But that crucial play, and its outcome, was about more than Yelich's impressive read and instincts. His footspeed from first to second clocked in at 28.5 mph, a full tick faster than his season average. That's an 81st-percentile result from a 34-year-old DH with a history of back problems.
Yelich was once a speedster before age and injuries did their thing. There exists a timeline in which the 2018 MVP evolved into a bat-first baseclogger, a plodder focused on in-box responsibilities. Instead, Yelich has done everything in his power to remain as athletic, as lithe and as quick as possible. Years of treatment, offseason sprint work, healthy habits, weight room sessions — all of it has allowed Yelich to maintain his speed despite the barrage of injuries and his status as a primary DH.
"I've got some things that have happened to me, but for the most part, I feel pretty good," he said when asked about his speed. "I feel like I can still hang with the boys out there."
The boys agree.
"That baserunning by Yeli there, which allowed us to have that huge inning ..." outfielder Sal Frelick said. "We work on those things in spring. He's the guy that's running the meeting, saying this is important. It's his 14th season. He's been All-Star, Silver Slugger, MVP, and nobody cares about baserunning more than him. Just to see him do that, get a good secondary, run as hard as he could and beat that out — that's what allowed us to have that big inning."
"Little things like that — that's what makes our team great."
Great might be an understatement. If the Brewers finish the deal in Game 4, they would become the first team in the League Championship Series era to sweep both the championship series and World Series rounds. They would finish this month a mind-boggling 11-1, with their only defeat coming by one run in NLDS Game 3 in San Diego. There's a strong argument that we are currently witnessing the most dominant postseason team in MLB history.
The gap between these Brewers and the rest of the league is a massive chasm, yes, but it's one they chiseled one swing and one step at a time.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays are favored to take Game 3 on Monday, but their chances of capturing their first ever World Series title have dwindled.
The Rays jumped out to a 4-0 first inning lead in Game 2, but through the game’s final eight innings the offense sputtered and the defense, nor pitching from ace Drew Rasmussen, was as sharp as needed to hold down the Brewers, who earned a 5-4 victory.
The pair of one-run victories in Milwaukee have put the Brewers in prime position for their first title. Nearly 81% of MLB teams that have generated a 2-0 series lead in the World Series have gone on to win the title.
To disrupt that statistic, the Rays will need to find a way to win Game 3. Kalshi traders make their odds 53% as of Monday morning.
For informational purposes only. Not trading advice. See full disclaimer below. Kalshi is the Official Prediction Market Partner of the Atlanta Braves, Los Angeles Dodgers, San Francisco Giants, San Diego Padres, and Boston Red Sox.
World Series Game 3 Odds: Rays favored in home ballpark
Right-handed pitcher Freddy Peralta had a rough start to his 2026 campaign when pitching for the New York Mets. But after being dealt to the Rays, he’s unlocked a former version of himself, one the Milwaukee Brewers know quite well. Peralta pitched for the Brewers for eight seasons before being traded to the Mets in the offseason. The Mets dealt him to the Rays at the trade deadline.
As such, now he’ll need to square off against his former team in World Series Game 3, looking to extend an incredible stretch of pitching which saw him earn ALCS MVP honors.
Across three starts and one relief appearance this postseason, Peralta has thrown 16.2 innings and allowed just two earned runs, good for a 1.08 ERA.
But the Brewers represent a level up offensively. Milwaukee finished the regular season tied for first in wRC+ against right-handed starters and led the league in on-base percentage and batting average against the handedness.
On the other hand, the Rays will draw left-handed starter Robert Gasser. Like the rest of the Milwaukee staff, Gasser has been fantastic this postseason, throwing nine innings over the course of two starts and allowing just one earned run.
Southpaws have been a challenge for the Rays this season, with the team ranking 26th against lefties in terms of wRC+ during the regular season. Even if they are able to get through Gasser, the Milwaukee bullpen features lefties JoJo Romero, DL Hall, and Aaron Ashby, and has been nearly unhittable, collectively posting a 1.23 ERA in nearly 51 innings this postseason.
Nevertheless, Kalshi traders make the Rays, who posted a 55-26 record at home during the regular season, slight favorites at 53% in Game 3.
The Rays overcame a 2-1 deficit in the ALCS, but they face a stiffer test against baseball’s top team in the World Series.
Regardless of the Game 3 winner, Game 4 will take place on Tuesday in Tampa Bay. In early trading, Kalshi traders make the Brewers slight favorites on the road in that game, pricing them at 50%.
Should a Game 5 be necessary, it will take place on Wednesday in Tampa Bay. If Games 6 or 7 are required, those will take place back in Milwaukee after a travel day.
Through two games, Brewers catcher William Contreras is the favorite for World Series MVP, according to Kalshi traders.
Contreras is trading around 38% to earn the award while outfielder Jackson Chourio is trading at 17% and left-handed reliever Aaron Ashby is priced at 15%.
In their two home victories, Contreras has notched four hits in eight at-bats and driven in two runs for Milwaukee. Plus, he’s thrown out multiple runners attempting to steal and helped manage a pitching staff through two tense one-run victories.
Chourio has posted similar stats, netting four hits in his nine at-bats, while stealing two bases and cutting down a runner at the plate with an outfield assist during Game 2.
Though less heralded coming into the series, Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby has been dominant all postseason, pitching 15.2 innings without allowing a single run. That includes more than three innings of World Series play in which he’s only allowed one hit.
Down 2-0, the highest priced Ray player is Junior Caminero, who is trading around 6% to win the award.

Happy Monday, everyone! The World Series got underway this weekend, and it hasn’t felt particularly close at all so far. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are coming off another strong regular season.
That said, they also had another letdown in the postseason.
After sweeping the Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, the Yankees got swept by the Tampa Bay Rays in the ALDS.
They lost the final game (at home in the Bronx) by a score of 4-3.
New York Yankees Will Pay 34-Year-Old $27 Million
With the season over, it’s worth taking a look at Carlos Rodon.
The 33-year-old (who will turn 34 in December) is coming off a strong regular season.
He went 7-3 with a 2.67 ERA in 16 starts.
Chris Kirschner of The Athletic wrote (on September 16): “Carlos Rodón, who regained some velocity as his outing progressed, has not allowed more than three runs in 25 straight starts. It is the longest streak in Yankees history and tied for the sixth-longest streak in MLB history.”
Carlos Rodon #55 of the New York Yankees delivers a pitch in the first inning against the New York Mets at Yankee Stadium on September 11, 2026 in The Bronx borough of New York City. The New York Yankees and the New York Mets are wearing hats to honor first responders on the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 attack on New York during the game.
It’s also worth mentioning that the Yankees still owe Rodon a lot of money.
He will be paid $27 million during the 2027 season (h/t Spotrac).
ESPN’s Jeff Passan wrote (on December 15, 2022): “Left-hander Carlos Rodón and the New York Yankees are in agreement on a six-year, $162 million contract, sources familiar with the deal tell ESPN.”
Rodon will become a free agent following the 2028 MLB season.
Looking At Rodon
Carlos Rodon #55 of the New York Yankees pitches in the fourth inning against the Baltimore Orioles at Oriole Park at Camden Yards on August 18, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland.
Rodon was picked in the 1st round of the 2014 MLB Draft.
He spent the first seven years of his career playing for the Chicago White Sox.
After Chicago, Rodon (who is a three-time MLB All-Star) had a quick stint with the San Francisco Giants.
Samantha Busch, Ashley Rodón and Carlos Rodón attend the Carlos Rodón Foundation 2026 Willow Gala at the Refinery on August 24, 2026 in Brooklyn, New York.
Rodon has 100 career wins with a 3.67 ERA.

item.title: [House That Hank Built] Matt Olson’s Fielding Bible win puts Braves first baseman in rare company
item.dc:creator: Steven Teal
item.description: Award season is upon us, and the Atlanta Braves have already secured some hardware. It stinks not to see the team in the playoffs, but there were some great performances shown to fans this season. Matt Olson was unsurprisingly among the players who gave fans something to cheer about. His time at the plate was inconsistent at times, but he still put up respectable numbers. item.content:encoded:
Award season is upon us, and the Atlanta Braves have already secured some hardware. It stinks not to see the team in the playoffs, but there were some great performances shown to fans this season. Matt Olson was unsurprisingly among the players who gave fans something to cheer about. His time at the plate was inconsistent at times, but he still put up respectable numbers.
Atlanta's first baseman had a .251/.321/.502 slash line, with 34 doubles, 41 home runs, 93 RBI, and a 122 wRC+. Those are great numbers, but he disappeared in the postseason, which was tough to watch. The offense is one aspect of Olson's impressive game, but his defense remained elite in 2026. His impressive fielding work led to his first award of the season. Olson was awarded a Fielding Bible Award to recognize him as the best defensive first baseman in baseball.
The Fielding Bible Awards are handed out each season to one player at each of the nine positions as the top fielder in MLB at that position. They also award one "multi-position" player, one overall Defensive Player of the Year, and a Defensive Team of the Year. Recipients are voted on by a panel of experts based on a combination of stats, the eye test, and any other factors the voters choose to consider.
Matt Olson's latest defensive honor a reminder of his underrated skill set
Olson was in a tight race with Padres first baseman Ty France this season. However, his incredible OAA and FRV set him apart. He finished the season with an 11 outs above average (OAA) and 12 fielding run value (FRV). Those numbers were both the best in baseball among all first basemen. France edged out Olson in defensive runs saved (DRS), with 15 DRS compared to Olson's 11 DRS.
This win was Olson's sixth Fielding Bible Award at first base, which surpassed Albert Pujols for the most wins at the position. Atlanta's lefty slugger is now tied with Yadier Molina and Andrelton Simmons for the second-most all-time wins among all positions. Olson only trails Mookie Betts, who has seven wins, for the most Fielding Bible Awards.
It likely won't be the last award for Olson, who is also nominated for a Gold Glove Award this season. He continues to be a wonderful addition for the Braves.

item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers won Game 1 of the World Series behind a solid start from Jacob Misiorowski. He went five innings and picked up the win.
It was Misiorowski's longest start of the postseason, and he was the Brewers' first starting pitcher to get a win in the postseason. The 24-year-old is poised to win the National League Cy Young Award in the coming weeks, and on Friday, he became the youngest starting pitcher since Jaret Wright to get a win in Game 1 of the World Series.
Wright's win came in 1997 when Cleveland played the Florida Marlins. He was 21 years old at the time.
It really puts into perspective how hard it is to pitch well on the biggest stage as a young pitcher. Misiorowski has been lighting up the radar gun this October, but he has been nowhere near as dominant as he was in the regular season.
The Brewers threw their best arm in Game 1, but the Tampa Bay Rays did not. Misiorowski will be lined up to pitch in Game 5, while Drew Rasmussen looks like he will pitch in Game 2 and Game 6, should the series get there.
However,. depending on how the series goes, the Brewers and Rays could both move where their aces are slated to pitch.
More MLB: Brewers GM, Manager Offer Vague Responses When Asked About Brandon Woodruff's Role

item.title: [trentonian.com] World Series: Brewers withstand Rays’ comeback attempt to win Game 1
item.dc:creator: Steve Megargee

item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE (AP) — Trevor Megill was shouting in celebration and the Milwaukee Brewers were bolting out of the dugout to congratulate one another, believing they had just escaped a ninth-inning jam to win Game 1 of the World Series.
Not quite yet.
What initially was ruled a game-ending double play got overturned after a video review showed Brewers shortstop Cooper Pratt’s right foot was slightly off the bag when he reached to catch a high throw from second baseman Brice Turang.
No problem.
Megill regrouped and struck out Jonny DeLuca with two runners in scoring position as Milwaukee edged the Tampa Bay Rays 3-2 on Friday night.
“It’s good to get the first win out of the way,” Megill said. “That’s where all the nerves are at. First game, a lot of anticipation and build-up to where we are right now.”
The ninth inning was particularly nerve-racking for the Brewers and the sellout crowd attending Milwaukee’s first World Series game since 1982.
“You have a big range of emotions,” said team captain Christian Yelich, whose RBI triple in the first put the Brewers ahead for good. “It’s a big credit to Trev for locking back in right there and making some huge pitches after you have that emotional dump and then have to get back on it.”
Tampa Bay trailed 3-1 and hadn’t put a runner on since the sixth until it mounted its comeback attempt against Megill.
Jonathan Aranda, who went 3 for 3 with a walk, and Chandler Simpson hit consecutive one-out singles. A double steal involving pinch-runner Jorge Mateo and Simpson put runners on second and third before Junior Caminero walked on a 3-2 pitch in the dirt to load the bases.
Liam Hicks hit a grounder to the right side, and Turang ranged well to his left to field the ball before throwing to Pratt to start what initially was called a 4-6-3 double play.
Fireworks went off, players poured onto the field and Milwaukee fans roared. But then the crowd hushed as it watched the play again on the videoboard.
“You’ve got to think worst-case scenario there,” Megill said. “I thought the challenge was at first base, maybe a bobble or something. But it was pretty clear once the replay went up that it was on the play at second base. Zoomed in and it didn’t look good. It’s all right. We picked up Cooper there. He’ll pick us up tomorrow.”
The out call at second was changed to safe by umpire Alfonso Márquez at the MLB Replay Center, which caught Pratt by surprise.
“Obviously, it was close,” the 22-year-old rookie said. “I just didn’t think it was enough to overturn, so I wasn’t thinking anything of it. The video I saw, thought my cleat was dragging. … There must have been some other angles that I haven’t seen. It ultimately didn’t matter because we won.”
The Brewers won because Megill got DeLuca to swing and miss at a 2-2 pitch, capping a night in which Tampa Bay went 0 for 6 with runners in scoring position.
“This is an extremely confident group,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “You know that. We know that. They’re going to be fine. I think the frustration comes from we were one swing of the bat away right at the end of potentially taking the lead.”
The Game 1 winner has gone on to win the World Series 62.8% of the time.
This marks the first World Series featuring two teams seeking their first championship since 1980, when the Philadelphia Phillies beat the Kansas City Royals in six games. The only other major league clubs without a World Series title are the Colorado Rockies, San Diego Padres and Seattle Mariners.
Milwaukee took a 2-0 lead in the first inning against Nick Martinez. NL Cy Young Award favorite Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run and four hits over five innings to help the Brewers stay in front before relievers Abner Uribe and Aaron Ashby shut down the Rays through the eighth.
Misiorowski, who had a season-low three strikeouts, opened the game with a 103.5 mph fastball — the fastest pitch ever thrown in a World Series.
“The adrenaline kind of took over, and I tensed up and threw it hard,” said Misiorowski, who earned the win. “Then I settled down, and that was the game plan, to settle in and do me. Don’t try and overdo it.”
Milwaukee’s Jackson Chourio and William Contreras each had two hits, including an RBI single. Contreras also threw out two runners trying to steal.
Tampa Bay managed to hang around thanks in part to Martinez, who gave up those two runs in the first but held Milwaukee scoreless through the rest of his five-inning stint. The Brewers added an insurance run in the seventh when Chourio singled home Pratt.
Then came all the action in the ninth, with the Brewers’ premature celebration followed by a team-wide sigh of relief as Pratt offered some parting words to Megill.
“I just said, ‘Thank you, man. Thanks for picking me up,’” Pratt said. “That’s what this game is. It’s a game of pick-me-up. He picked me up today.”
Up next
Drew Rasmussen (16-5, 2.67 ERA) pitches for Tampa Bay and Logan Henderson (11-3, 2.47) starts for Milwaukee in Game 2 on Saturday night. In this postseason, Rasmussen is 2-0 with a 1.29 ERA and Henderson is 0-0 with a 3.00 ERA.

item.title: [News4JAX] Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski sets World Series velocity record on his first pitch
item.dc:creator: Ronald Blum; Associated Press
item.description: MILWAUKEE – Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other. “I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said. Recommended Videos He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic. The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5 mph fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Díaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. item.content:encoded:
MILWAUKEE – Jacob Misiorowski stepped on the mound for a World Series debut like no other.
“I had so much adrenaline built up,” he said.
Recommended Videos
He threw a pitch the likes of which had never been seen in the Fall Classic.
The Miz broke the World Series velocity record with his very first delivery, a 103.5 mph fastball to the Tampa Bay Rays’ Yandy Díaz that was taken high out of the strike zone for a ball. He allowed one run over five innings to get his first postseason win as a starter, helping the Milwaukee Brewers to a 3-2 victory in Friday night’s opener.
“I don’t even know how to tell you how I felt,” the 24-year-old right-hander said a half-hour after the end of a crazy ninth inning, prolonged by a game-extending video review. “I still don’t know how I felt. I feel like I’m still trying to take everything in and understand what happened.”
Misiorowski gave up four hits and one walk, striking out a season-low three.
Aroldis Chapman of the Chicago Cubs had the previous mark for fastest Series pitch at 103.2 mph in the ninth inning of Game 2 in 2016, an offering that resulted in a groundout to second by Cleveland’s Coco Crisp. The previous high by a Series starting pitcher since tracking began in 2008 was 101.1 mph by the New York Mets’ Noah Syndergaard to Kansas City’s Ben Zobrist that was taken for a ball in the first inning of Game 3 in 2015.
Miz reached 100 mph with 38 pitches, topping the previous Series high of 24 by Chapman in Game 5 of 2016. The most by a starting pitcher in the Series had been six by Tampa Bay’s Tyler Glasnow in the 2020 opener against the Los Angeles Dodgers.
Tampa Bay scored in the fourth when Jonathan Aranda walked, took third on Junior Caminero’s double over center fielder Garrett Mitchell and came around on Liam Hicks’ grounder to first baseman Jake Bauers.
Nearing the end of his first full major league season, Misiorowski has reached 100 mph with 134 of 260 postseason pitches. But his spin rate was down, a sign of a season in which he has pitched 188 innings — up from 141 1/3 innings last year. And he got just seven swings and misses, five on his fastball.
Tampa Bay batters fouled off 20 of his 78 pitches and tipped another.
During the regular season, Misiorowski reached 100 mph with 1,115 pitches, including a high of 105.5 mph to the Chicago Cubs’ Pete Crow-Armstrong on June 27.
“What we’re used to seeing in the regular season was Miz just mow through people and have two strikeouts an inning. That’s unrealistic,” Brewers manager Pat Murphy said. “This is the best team in the American League.”
Miz's first pitch was so fast the scoreboard at American Family Field couldn't keep up, flashing 103.4 mph — one-tenth of a mile less than it registered on MLB’s Statcast system.
“He’s such a special pitcher,” Rays manager Kevin Cash said. “I felt like for him to be out of the game at five innings, there’s a small win in that.”
Misiorowski threw fastballs on 10 of his first 12 pitches, then mixed in more offspeed stuff. In all he tossed 48 fastballs, 17 cutters, seven sliders and six curveballs.
Miz finished with 30 pitches at 101 mph or higher, 11 of 102 mph or more and three at 103-plus mph.
Warming up in the bullpen, he couldn't take in the introductions before Milwaukee's first World Series game in 44 years. He thought about how far he had come, how he was at Double-A Biloxi two years ago.
“It was crazy," he said. “It’s everything I dreamed of.”
___

item.content:encoded:
Brewers' Jacob Misiorowski drops brutally honest admission on his Game 1 start appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Milwaukee Brewers possessed a top-notch bullpen in the regular season and in the last two rounds of the playoffs, but the idea of this team winning a championship without Jacob Misiorowski posting his best stuff seemed near-incomprehensible. The presumptive National League Cy Young was unable to reach the sixth inning for a third straight postseason start, and yet, the Brew Crew are now just three wins away from capturing their first World Series title in franchise history.
Misiorowski pitched five innings of one-run ball in Friday's 3-2 Game 1 victory versus the Tampa Bay Rays, allowing four hits while recording three strikeouts and one walk. He perfectly described his fairly short yet triumphant outing.
"Not perfect, good enough to get a win," the genial 24-year-old right-hander said, via Joey Mistretta of ClutchPoints.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Misiorowski has not been operating as a work horse for some time. He has accumulated only a combined 13 1/3 innings of work across three playoff outings. The three Ks are also surprisingly low. This record-breaking flamethrower is nearing the end of his first full MLB campaign, and he is showing the effects of unleashing elite velocity all yearlong.
Like Misiorowski said, though, he had enough on this night. The Brewers' bullpen also provided first-class reinforcements, once again. Aaron Ashby remains unstoppable, Abner Uribe enjoyed a stellar showing in his own right and Trevor Megill survived despite allowing one run in the ninth. The lineup notched timely hits, as it does, and All-Star catcher William Contreras threw out potential game-tying runs multiple times.
Jacob Misiorowski did not carry the squad to a 1-0 series lead in American Family Field. Pat Murphy has not asked him to fill that role during this postseason. Milwaukee secured the W by putting forth a complete effort. This ballclub may not have many household names, but it should be obvious by now that one player does not define Brewers baseball.
If Milwaukee has its way, Misiorowski will not have to put the team on his back again for the rest of 2026. Game 2 is Saturday at approximately 8 p.m. ET.

item.title: [dairylandexpress.com] Pat Murphy throws the Rays a curveball with Brewers' batting order in World Series Game 1
item.dc:creator: Dylan Carter
item.description: If you expected the Milwaukee Brewers to enter the World Series without making any adjustments, you must not have been watching the team this season. Even after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and overcoming a red-hot Padres squad in the Division Series, manager Pat Murphy is always finding new ways to keep his opponents on their toes. The Brewers released their batting order on Friday afternoon, just hours before first pitch. Their updated order will be as follows: 1. Jackson Chour
item.content:encoded:
If you expected the Milwaukee Brewers to enter the World Series without making any adjustments, you must not have been watching the team this season. Even after sweeping the Los Angeles Dodgers in the NLCS and overcoming a red-hot Padres squad in the Division Series, manager Pat Murphy is always finding new ways to keep his opponents on their toes.
The Brewers released their batting order on Friday afternoon, just hours before first pitch. Their updated order will be as follows:
1. Jackson Chourio
2. Jake Bauers
3. Christian Yelich
4. William Contreras
5. Brice Turang
6. Garrett Mitchell
7. Cooper Pratt
8. Sal Frelick
9. David Hamilton
What should we take away from the Milwaukee Brewers' updated batting order for Game 1 of the World Series?
This new-look order should give the Brewers an interesting dynamic of staggering lefty and righty batters, likely in hopes of keeping Game 1 starter Nick Martinez, a righty, out of a consistent rhythm to begin the contest. By moving Contreras to fourth, it sets up Milwaukee's best home run hitter this postseason for a grand slam opportunity, should it arise. Meanwhile, Yelich at the third spot gives the Brew Crew a likely opportunity for some much-needed contact hitting early in the rotation.
It's far from surprising to see first baseman Jake Bauers taking such a firm position near the top of the batting order, as Bauers emerged as one of the most reliable offensive threats on the team, and frankly, in all of baseball. His ability to extend the pitch count and make contact persistently has been a thorn in the sides of pitchers everywhere, so this is likely Murphy's best attempt to extend Martinez's pitch count early.
Meanwhile, Turang slotting back into the fifth spot in the lineup makes sense given his inconsistent production thus far in the postseason. Through eight games, the 26-year-old is hitting just .222 with six hits to seven strikeouts. The good news, however, is that Turang turned a corner in the Dodgers series, logging hits in three of four hits, while scoring a run in each contest.
The end of the lineup should be of interest as well. All year long, Brewers fans grappled with questions over David Hamilton's place in the lineup, but through the postseason, he's certainly proving he belongs. Milwaukee is in serious need of some production late in the order, so all eyes will be on Hamilton, as well as Cooper Pratt and Sal Frelick, to carry that torch.
Overall, this is a wise move by Pat Murphy to make sure his lineup isn't identical to what Tampa Bay was expecting to see. Although the players are the same, a little shake-up in the order might force Martinez and the Rays' defense to think twice, which is all the Brewers can really ask for in a matchup of two teams that are this talented defensively.

item.content:encoded:
Another season is coming to a close – the World Series is here. The Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays, both vying for their first championship. Who do we think will win? In how many games? Who will get MVP? Here are our thoughts.
As someone who married into a family of Rays fans and will be in Florida with my wife’s family for Halloween I would love to say the Rays will win in seven and I will watch that game with her family, but it is hard to vote against the Brewers.
They have the better offense. They have the better starting pitching. They have the deeper bullpen. They may even be better defensively. And they are going to be a bit more rested.
Because I will be on an airplane for game six I will say that the Brewers will win in six games.
The fun WSMVP choice would be Aaron Ashby continuing to dominate and taking the award by storm but a reliever has not won the WSMVP since Mariano Rivera in 1999 and Ashby is not the team’s primary closer.
So I will go with Jacob Misiorowski throwing two elite starts in games one and five, as well as an impact relief appearance in game six.
I think these teams are pretty evenly matched – the Rays have the upper hand in starting pitching, the Brewers have the better bullpen. While the Brewers scored more runs in the regular season, the teams had similar rate stats (Milwaukee had a 105 OPS+, compared to Tampa Bay’s 103). The Rays’ starters have consistently worked deeper into games compared to Milwaukee, and I wonder at what point the wear and tear will start to get to the Brewers’ bullpen. The Rays don’t strike out often, which leads me to believe they can be the team that finally conquers Milwaukee’s relievers. Milwaukee’s offense was relentless against the Dodgers, so it won’t be easy for the Rays to keep the Brewers down.
Overall, I think this will be a hard-fought series, with the Rays emerging victorious in seven games. Drew Rasmussen will win World Series MVP, winning his starts in Game 1 and Game 5, then coming out of the bullpen to pitch in Game 7.
Brewers in 7, Jackson Chourio is MVP. I wish Bob Uecker was here to see it.
Brewers in six. This should be a really fun and competitive series between two teams who play baseball the right way. Pitching wins, especially in the postseason, so Jacob Misiorowski will win the MVP after authoring his postseason legacy with two elite starts and a gutsy appearance out of the bullpen with everything on the line.
Brewers in 6. Christian Yelich wins MVP as he lives up to his newly minted captain status. Tampa will give them a run for their money!
Rays in 7. Freddy Peralta World Series MVP, because why not. He enters in desperation relief to get the final out.
