item.title: [fansided.com] Rays and Brewers set for World Series showdown in updated MLB playoff bracket
item.dc:creator: Chris Landers
item.description: Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history. Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise histo
item.content:encoded:
Just days ago, the Tampa Bay Rays were trailing the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS two games to one. Three straight wins later, they're back in the World Series for the second time in seven years and the third time in franchise history.
Which means that now, our 2026 Fall Classic is officially set. And while it might not be the big-market showdown of Rob Manfred's dreams, it should be absolutely box-office baseball, as the two best teams of this season square off to try and make franchise history. Let's dive in.
Updated MLB playoff bracket after Rays advance to the World Series
And then there were two. The Milwaukee Brewers punched their ticket to the World Series seemingly eons ago, dispatching of the Los Angeles Dodgers in a shocking sweep. Now that the Rays have knocked off the Guardians in the ALCS, our World Series matchup is set.
- World Series: Tampa Bay Rays (AL champs) vs. Milwaukee Brewers (NL champs)
It's not all that often that the top seed in each league meets in the Fall Classic; baseball's postseason is notoriously unpredictable. But these teams won 98 and 103 games in the regular season, respectively, and led the AL and NL more or less wire-to-wire. They were the best in baseball, and they proved as much in October. Now it's time to see which will make history and capture their franchise's first-ever World Series title.
Full World Series schedule: Milwaukee will be rocking for Game 1
We'll have a few days of waiting: Game 1 is set for Friday, Oct. 23, with first pitch from American Family Field in Milwaukee at 8 p.m. ET. The series will follow the traditional 2-3-2 format, with days off for travel after Games 2 and 5. Games 1, 2, 6 and 7 will be in Milwaukee, with Games 3-5 in Tampa.
| Game | Location | Date | Time |
|---|---|---|---|
| Game 1 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 23 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 2 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 24 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 3 | Tropicana Field | Monday, Oct. 26 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 4 | Tropicana Field | Tuesday, Oct. 27 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 5 | Tropicana Field | Wednesday, Oct. 28 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 6 | American Family Field | Friday, Oct. 30 | 8 p.m. ET |
| Game 7 | American Family Field | Saturday, Oct. 31 | 8 p.m. ET |
The Rays are grateful for the break, as it will allow them to reset their pitching staff and line ace Drew Rasmussen up to face off against Jacob Misiorowski in Game 1. Clinching on Monday also allows Freddy Peralta to potentially get the ball in Game 2 on Saturday on full rest, with Nick Martinez likely behind him in Game 3.
Of course, the last thing the Brewers need is more rest. They clinched the NLCS in Game 4 last Thursday, Oct. 15, meaning they've already been at home for four days. By the time Game 1 of the World Series rolls around, it'll have been over a week since they last played a competitive game. Rust is overblown this time of year, but it's still something to monitor.
How to watch the 2026 World Series
This year's World Series will be broadcast exclusively on FOX.
- Dates: Oct. 23-Oct. 31
- TV channel: FOX
- Streaming: FOX One, YouTube TV, Hulu + Live Sports
You can also stream all the action on FOX One, provided you have a Fox One subscription ($19.99/month) or a valid cable login. You can also stream FOX through a variety of platforms, from YouTube TV to Hulu to Sling TV — all of which have free trials for new customers.
Pitching and power will define Brewers-Rays matchup
Suffice to say that runs are going to be at a premium in this series. Milwaukee ranked second in baseball in team ERA during the regular season, while the Rays were seventh. With Misiorowski, Logan Henderson and the best bullpen in baseball on one side and Rasmussen, Peralta, Martinez and All-Star closer Bryan Baker on the other, these teams have arms for days.
As such, it's going to be awfully hard to string together rallies — which means the team that finds a way to access some power will be at a distinct advantage. Neither team played much long ball during the regular season; both ranked in the bottom third of the league in homers, and neither ranked in the top 10 in slugging percentage. But the Brewers actually outslugged the big, bad Dodgers in the NLCS, and the Rays pulled away from Cleveland when their big bats (Junior Caminero, Yandy Diaz and Jonathan Aranda) finally found the power stroke.
There won't be a ton of homers in this series. But whichever team has the most will almost certainly be hoisting the Commissioner's Trophy when all is said and done. If you're trying to play small ball against Abner Uribe, good luck.

item.title: [PCMag] Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays Livestream: How to Watch Today's MLB Playoff Game 6, Even for Free
item.dc:creator: Jason Cohen
item.description: As summer comes to a close and the air turns crisp, you know what's coming: the MLB Playoffs. From the universal DH and the pitch clock to video replay and an automated strike zone, baseball may look very different if you haven't been paying attention. The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time
item.content:encoded:
As summer comes to a close and the air turns crisp, you know what's coming: the MLB Playoffs. The NFL season is already underway, and if you're also a baseball lover, this next month is essential viewing. The MLB has been through a number of changes in recent years. From the universal DH and the pitch clock to video replay and an automated strike zone, baseball may look very different if you haven't been paying attention.
The Brewers swept the Dodgers to reach the World Series for the first time in 44 years. Now, it comes down to the Rays and Guardians in the best-of-seven Championship series. Which team will come out on top? Here's how you can watch live.
What Time Is the Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays Game?
Tonight's game between the Rays and Guardians will take place on Monday, October 19 at 8:08 p.m. ET.
How to Watch the Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays?
This year, the American League Division Series games will be broadcast on TBS. You can also watch them with a live TV or sports streaming subscription from DirecTV, Fubo, HBO Max, Hulu, Sling, Sportsnet+ (if you're in Canada), or YouTube TV. The World Series will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One app.
How to Watch the Guardians vs. Rays for Free
If you don't want to subscribe to any of the above platforms, you may be able to sign up for a few free trials to gain access to the remaining games. Fox One and Hulu offer three-day trials, DirecTV and Fubo offer five days, and YouTube TV gives you 10 days for free.
2026 MLB Playoffs Game Schedule
MLB's expanded postseason means more teams on the playoff schedule. Things started off with the best-of-three Wild Card Series, where the Braves, Padres, White Sox, and Yankees advanced. The best-of-five Division Series put them up against the Los Angeles Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Cleveland Guardians, and Tampa Bay Rays, respectively. All of whom managed to advance.
The Brewers beat the Dodgers in four games. Now, it comes down to the Rays and Guardians in the best-of-seven Championship Series to determine the best team in the American League. The winner will meet Milwaukee in the best-of-seven World Series to begin on October 23. Who will make it all the way?
Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays - TBR lead 3-2
- Game 6 on October 19 @ 5 p.m. ET - TBS/HBO Max
- Game 7 on October 20 @ 8 p.m. ET - TBS/HBO Max*
*if necessary
World Series: Milwaukee Brewers vs. TBD
- Game 1 on October 23 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 2 on October 24 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 3 on October 26 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 4 on October 27 - Fox/Fox One
- Game 5 on October 28 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 6 on October 30 - Fox/Fox One*
- Game 7 on October 31 - Fox/Fox One*
*if necessary
How to Stream the 2026 MLB Playoffs
This year's MLB postseason is stretched across multiple networks and streaming services. All Wild Card Series games for the American League and National League were broadcast on NBC, NBCSN, and Peacock. Additional rounds will be on other networks. ALDS and ALCS games are on TBS/TruTV and HBO Max, while NLDS and NLCS games were on Fox/FS1. For the World Series, all games will be broadcast on Fox and the Fox One streaming service.
- DirecTV: DirecTV's MySports base pack costs $45 per month for the first six months to see every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, and TBS/TruTV.
- Fox One: Fox's own streaming app lets you watch the NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox and FS1 for $20 per month.
- Fubo: Fubo's Sports plan costs $45.99 for the first month to watch the Wild Card Series, NLDS, NLCS, and World Series on Fox, FS1, and NBC/NBCSN.
- HBO Max: If you pay for the $18.49-per-month HBO Max Standard, you'll be able to watch the ALDS and ALCS games on TBS/TruTV.
- Hulu: For $90 per month, you can watch every game on Fox, FS1, NBC, TBS, and TruTV.
- Peacock: Instead of a live TV service, you'd need to pay $10.99 per month for Peacock Premium to see the Wild Card Series games.
- Sling: The $60.99-per-month Sling Orange & Blue bundle will let you watch the ALDS and ALCS on TBS/TruTV and the NLDS and NLCS on FS1. Day Passes are also available for Sling Orange, allowing you to watch games on TBS for up to seven days.
- Sportsnet+ (Canada only): The $30-per-month Standard tier lets you watch every postseason game.
- YouTube TV: Though the standard plan for YouTube TV costs $83 per month, you can actually now pay for the cheaper $65 Sports package to see all games on Fox, FS1, NBC/NBCSN, and TBS/TruTV.
Can I Watch Postseason Games on MLB.TV?
Are you already an MLB.TV subscriber? You can watch the Division Series, Championship Series, and World Series games through MLB's own streaming service—but there's a catch. To watch on MLB.TV, you'll first need to authenticate through a participating pay TV provider. It's such a sticking point that it makes the entire question moot. If you already have a TV provider, then you wouldn't need to use a streaming service. If you don't already have an MLB.TV subscription, don't pay for one now.
How can I listen to the 2026 postseason?
You can also listen to the games via ESPN Radio.
Which Teams Are In the Playoffs?
Since MLB expanded its postseason picture in 2022, a total of 12 teams make the playoffs each year. That includes six teams per league, including the three division winners and three Wild Card teams.
- American League Division Winners: Tampa Bay Rays (1), Cleveland Guardians (2), Houston Astros (3)
- American League Wild Card: New York Yankees (4), Boston Red Sox (5), Chicago White Sox (6)
- National League Division Winners: Milwaukee Brewers (1), Los Angeles Dodgers (2), Atlanta Braves (3)
- National League Wild Card: Chicago Cubs (4), Philadelphia Phillies (5), San Diego Padres (6)
Upgrade Your Streaming Experience
If you decide to watch the MLB postseason, there's still time to get a big-screen television for viewing this beautiful game. Pro tip: Turn on your TV's motion-smoothing option for the best picture while watching sports. Just remember to turn it off before watching other TV shows and movies to avoid the awful "soap opera" effect.
About Our Expert
As PCMag's editor of how to content, I have to cover a wide variety of topics and also make our stories accessible to everyday users. Considering my history as a technical writer, copywriter, and all-around freelancer covering baseball, comics, and more at various outlets, I am used to making myself into an expert.
I believe tech corporations are bad, but you might as well know how to use technology in everyday life. Want more how to content delivered right to your inbox? Sign up for the tips and tricks newsletter that I curate three times a week.
My job as how-to guru means I use just about every gadget under the sun, so I can figure out how everything works. I work from a Lenovo ThinkPad running Windows 11, but also have a very large Dell Inspiron 17 3000 and Apple silicon MacBook. I have a Google Pixel 6a for personal use and use a Galaxy Z Flip 4 for additional Samsung-related testing. For iOS coverage, an iPhone 13 mini works like a charm, though it's already becoming a little long in the tooth.
My desktop situation includes a dual monitor setup with a modest Acer monitor. I also use a Logitech vertical mouse (who can use these ThinkPad trackpads) and a Havit keyboard (my first mechanical keyboard; I love it but my wife hates it!). I'm a recent convert from wired headphones; I have Anker Soundcore Liberty Air wireless earbuds for personal use and have taken to the Sennheiser HD 450BT headphones for work.
Whenever I have a second to myself, I'm probably gaming on my Nintendo Switch 2, Steam Deck, or Xbox Series S. I also still have a bunch of classic consoles lying around as well.

item.title: [Jays Journal] Alejandro Kirk’s Blue Jays World Series run is inspiring AL East rival Jonathan Aranda
item.dc:creator: Matthew Sookram
item.description: Alejandro Kirk has always been one of the most likeable players in the Toronto Blue Jays clubhouse. His steady presence, team-first approach and easygoing personality have made him a trusted teammate. But Kirk’s “Mr. Nice Guy” influence isn't limited to the guys who wear the same uniform as him. It has extended across the American League East, where Kirk’s longtime friend Jonathan Aranda is trying to help the Tampa Bay Rays capture their first World Series title. With the pressure of the postsea
item.content:encoded:
Alejandro Kirk has always been one of the most likeable players in the Toronto Blue Jays clubhouse. His steady presence, team-first approach and easygoing personality have made him a trusted teammate. But Kirk’s “Mr. Nice Guy” influence isn't limited to the guys who wear the same uniform as him.
It has extended across the American League East, where Kirk’s longtime friend Jonathan Aranda is trying to help the Tampa Bay Rays capture their first World Series title.
With the pressure of the postseason mounting, Aranda turned to his childhood friend who had just lived through the grind of a pressure packed postseason. During the Blue Jays’ run to the 2025 World Series Kirk played in all 18 games and slashed .254/.349/.493 with a 132 wRC+ and five home runs.
“I was like, ‘Hey, do you have any tips for me moving forward here in October?’ And his main suggestion was, just have fun, just have fun and be yourself,” Aranda told Sportsnet’s Shi Davidi through interpreter Kevin Vera ahead of Game 5 of the ALCS. “That's honestly helped me a lot to kind of slow the game down and enjoy the moment and embrace this challenge of what is October baseball.”
That advice could not have come at a better time for the Rays' Aranda who went 0-for-10 through the first three games of the best-of-seven series against the Cleveland Guardians. Then in Game 4 he broke out with three hits, a walk, two RBI and two runs scored in the Rays’ 7-3 win.
Kirk’s advice allowed Arenda some time to reflect on the process how to revive himself and be the player everyone expected him to be. He encouraged Aranda to trust himself and remember why he was there. The 28-year-old first baseman hit 22 home runs during the regular season while slashing .274/.358/.434 with a 123 wRC+ and a13.8 offensive fWAR.
Longtime friends Alejandro Kirk and Jonathan Aranda have always supported each other
For Kirk, helping a player on a division rival didn't seem like a conflict considering the Blue Jays bowed out of the postseason before it even began. Aranda said the two “talk every day, we're best friends, we're brothers,” adding that Kirk is “someone that I have by my side.”
The support has always worked both ways. When the Blue Jays advanced to the World Series last year, Aranda flew in to support Kirk, saying “it was a big thing for me to go see him, for us, to see each other in the World Series.”
Watching Kirk make history on baseball’s biggest stage gave Aranda a chance to picture himself playing October baseball. He said, “In that moment last year, I kind of visualized myself in the same scenario. So now, fast-forward a year later, I use it as motivation right now. Hopefully I can make those dreams that I had last year a reality and help this team to a World Series berth.”
The Blue Jays would rather see their own players carrying Kirk’s lessons deep into October. Still, his role in Aranda’s run says something meaningful about Kirk’s off-field qualities that don't show up in the scorebox every day.

item.content:encoded:
First pitch for the Cleveland Guardians vs. Tampa Bay Rays game is set for 8 p.m. ET on Monday, October 19 at Tropicana Field.
The Rays lead 3-2 in the American League Championship Series after defeating the Guardians 3-1 in Game 5 on Sunday. Tampa Bay can clinch a World Series berth with another win, while the Guardians need a road victory to force a decisive Game 7.
Freddy Peralta takes the mound for the Rays after delivering 6.0 scoreless innings against Cleveland in Game 2. The Guardians, meanwhile, face a challenging pitching situation after using their bullpen for 7.0 innings in Sunday's loss.
Below, we'll break down our Guardians vs. Rays prediction and picks for Monday's ALCS Game 6, including the winner and player picks for PrizePicks.
{{mlb_offer_banner="/style-system/ui-components-playbook"}}
Guardians vs. Rays Prediction, Spread, Over/Under for ALCS Game 6 – Monday, October 19
Tampa Bay enters Game 6 as the home favorites against the Guardians, returning a 1.63x payout if they win outright.
Here are the full payouts for the Guardians vs. Rays game on PrizePicks.
Team Picks data is live at the time of writing and is subject to change.
Peralta (0.79 ERA since August 26) will take the ball for Tampa Bay after delivering one of his best postseason performances in Game 2. The right-hander allowed just 4 hits and 2 walks while striking out 6, relying heavily on his four-seam fastball to overwhelm the Guardians.
Peralta (4.37 season xFIP) has been excellent since joining the Rays, going 5-2 with a 3.25 ERA. He's carried that momentum into October, allowing just a run over 10.2 postseason innings while recording 9 strikeouts.
He's rediscovered some of his early-career velocity, touching 99 MPH with his fastball in his last start.
Shawn Armstrong (2.35 postseason ERA) will open for Cleveland, with the Guardians facing elimination. The right-hander has been outstanding this October, allowing just 2 hits, recording 6 strikeouts, and issuing no walks over 7.2 scoreless innings.
However, Monday will mark his third appearance in as many days after he threw 1.1 scoreless innings in Game 5 and another scoreless frame in Game 4.
Cleveland will need significant bullpen contributions today. Regular-season starters SP Tanner Bibee and SP Joey Cantillo can provide length, while RP Hunter Gaddis, RP Erik Sabrowski, RP Tim Herrin, and closer Cade Smith could all factor in during the later innings.
One thing to note: SP Gavin Williams is unavailable on short rest after throwing 5.0 innings in Game 3, leaving the Guardians without their preferred starter in a must-win situation.
Cleveland's pitching staff must contain a Tampa Bay offense that's scored 10 runs over its last two games. The Guardians' relievers have performed well, but asking Armstrong to open for a third consecutive day before handing the ball to multiple pitchers creates a difficult challenge.
Guardians vs. Rays Prediction on Winner for ALCS Game 6 – 10/19/26
Here are the key stats and trends behind our Guardians vs. Rays prediction on the winner for Monday's ALCS Game 6.
Unless otherwise noted, data used in this article is from FanGraphs, Baseball Savant, and MLB.com.
- I like Tampa Bay to close out this series at home, a place where they've had tremendous success. The Rays went 58-27-0 straight up at home this season; their 68.2% home win rate ranks second in baseball behind the Milwaukee Brewers.
- Postseason baseball comes down to pitching, and the Rays are in a much better position when it comes to that. Peralta's already shut down the Guardians once, while Cleveland will rely on a bunch of bullpen arms worked to the bone.
- Peralta has fared much better at home all season, pitching to the tune of a 3.77 FIP compared to a 4.86 mark away from home.
- The Rays' offense has also been better at home, owning a 108 wRC+ at the Trop compared to 100 wRC+ on the road.
- Cleveland's wRC+ drops from 100 at home to 94 in road outings.
- Tampa Bay also has a slight bullpen advantage, owning the best relief xFIP in the postseason (2.80).

item.title: [MLB.com] LIVE on TBS/HBO Max: Rays-Guardians ALCS Game 5
item.dc:creator: Tim Stebbins; Keegan Matheson; Adam Berry
item.description: Sunday’s 5:08 p.m. ET game at Progressive Field will determine which side flies to St. Petersburg for Game 6 on the doorstep of the World Series and which team is fighting for their postseason lives. The Brewers get to kick their feet up and wait on the National League side, but over here in the American League, the stakes couldn’t be higher. The Rays are riding a high coming off their 7-3 win in Game 4, but as we’ve seen just about every day in this series, momentum can turn on a dime. The Guar
item.content:encoded:
Sunday’s 5:08 p.m. ET game at Progressive Field will determine which side flies to St. Petersburg for Game 6 on the doorstep of the World Series and which team is fighting for their postseason lives. The Brewers get to kick their feet up and wait on the National League side, but over here in the American League, the stakes couldn’t be higher.
The Rays are riding a high coming off their 7-3 win in Game 4, but as we’ve seen just about every day in this series, momentum can turn on a dime. The Guardians still feel like they’re playing their best baseball, going back to their incredible comeback to beat the White Sox in the ALDS, and they have a shot to take a commanding series lead in front of their home crowd Sunday.
“We're great. We're right in it. We're even,” said Guardians manager Stephen Vogt. “Again, now, it's a three-game series. I'll put our guys up against any team in the world in a three-game series. Of course, we would have loved to have taken a 3-to-1 lead tonight, but it's not in the cards. We can't control that now. We just show up, ready to play a good Game 5, and have a happy flight to Tampa.”
Drew Rasmussen will get the start for the Rays, and he’ll face Parker Messick, a premier pitching matchup on the biggest stage. These teams are starting to get aggressive, too, with the Rays using Freddy Peralta out of the bullpen in Game 4 while still keeping him available for later in the series.
The biggest threat to the Guardians now is the Rays’ Big Three of Junior Caminero, Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda, all of whom had big games in Game 4. Caminero’s was especially important, coming off four strikeouts in Game 3, and Aranda looks locked in. If that group can get back to Tropicana Field with a lead, look out.
“That was one of the main objectives that we had here coming into Cleveland, just to force the series back home,” Aranda said through interpreter Kevin Vera. “We're one of the best teams in the league when we're playing back on our home field, so we're going to use the fanbase and we're going to use that energy to push us forward. Drew is one of the best pitchers in the league, so it gives us a lot of confidence.”
After rain earlier this weekend, the forecast for Sunday is thankfully clear once again. It will still cool down as the evening stretches on, but the Guardians are used to these cold days, and the Rays, who play their home games under the dome at Tropicana Field, have already proven they can play in any environment.
When is the game and how can I watch it?
Game 5 of the Guardians-Rays ALDS is underway at Progressive Field. The game is being broadcast on TBS and HBO Max.
Spanish-language game broadcasts will be available on UniMas for the ALCS, and Spanish-language radio broadcasts will be available on Univision’s TUDN Radio.
Who are the starting pitchers?
Guardians: Parker Messick, LHP
Key stats: 5 IP, 6 H, 3 R, 0 ER, 2 BB, 3 K, 1 HBP in Game 2 
Messick started Game 2 on Tuesday, which initially lined him up to take the ball in Game 6 on Monday. The postponement that moved Game 4 from Friday to Saturday also moved Game 5 to Sunday, which allowed Messick to start this game on normal rest. The rookie lefty will be making his fourth postseason start; he logged a 3.09 ERA with eight walks and 14 strikeouts in 11 2/3 innings over his first three outings.
In a season where Messick emerged as an anchor in Cleveland’s rotation, this is among his biggest starts.
“To be able to take the ball in this game shows the confidence the team has in me,” Messick said. “Hopefully I'm able to go out there and do the job because I know how important it is going into opposing territory with a lead, one game away from heading to the World Series. I’m looking forward to the opportunity, and hopefully I do my best out there.”
Rays: Drew Rasmussen, RHP
Key stats: 14 IP, 2 R, 2 BB, 17 K in two postseason starts 
One benefit of the rainout? Rasmussen can start this game on five days’ rest, the way he made most of his starts during the regular season. The right-hander delivered a quality start in Tampa Bay’s Game 1 defeat, pitching into the seventh inning and ultimately allowing two runs while recording 18 outs. He was even better in Game 1 of the ALDS, when he struck out 10 while allowing just one hit over eight innings against the Yankees.
There’s nobody else the Rays would rather have on the mound with a chance to take the series lead before heading back home.
“It's still just baseball. I think that's led to a couple of successful outings up to this point,” Rasmussen said. “Just try and not make it anything bigger than what it actually is. It's you. It's preparation, and it's execution. Those are really the only things I'm concerned with.”
What are the starting lineups?
Guardians: Cleveland has kept a standard lineup this postseason, with the only change for Game 5 behind the plate. Though Austin Hedges had caught all but one of Messick’s starts this season and Patrick Bailey hadn’t caught him once, the Guardians wanted to get Bailey’s bat in the lineup as they attempt to take a 3-2 lead in the ALCS.
Rays: Tampa Bay slotted in Ryan Vilade in right field in place of Victor Mesa Jr. for a touch more right-handed punch against the left-handed Messick.
How will the bullpens line up after the starter?
Rays: Tampa Bay used five relievers behind starter Nick Martinez in Game 4, including presumptive Game 6 starter Freddy Peralta, but lefty Ian Seymour was the only one who threw more than 16 pitches. So expect the Rays to have everyone available between Rasmussen and closer Bryan Baker, who has finished each of Tampa Bay’s five postseason wins. Lefty Cam Booser has been the top left-handed option, right-hander Kevin Kelly gets most of the toughest right-handed matchups and setup man Tyler Wells asserted himself well with his two-inning appearance in Game 3. It’s possible that Griffin Jax, who started Game 3, could be called upon if needed. 
Guardians: Cleveland did not use closer Cade Smith and primary setup men Hunter Gaddis and Erik Sabrowski in the Game 4 loss. All three figure to factor into Game 5 as the Guardians look to take control of this series. In an ideal world, Messick will get Cleveland through five innings, if not six, and bridge the game to that trio.
Any injuries of note?
Rays: None.
Guardians: None.
Who is hot and who is not?
Rays: Simpson has been a spark plug of late, contributing a key single during the three-run rally in the fourth inning of Game 2 and then accounting for all of the team’s offense with his two-run triple in the fourth inning of Game 3. And the Big Three atop the order finally joined the party in Game 4, going 6-for-14 with five RBIs after a combined 5-for-34 start to the series. Maybe Hicks (3-for-20 in the postseason) and Mesa (4-for-25 with 11 strikeouts) will be the next ones to get going.
Guardians: Bazzana went 3-for-4 with a home run in Game 4. DeLauter’s first-inning RBI single in Game 4 was his 10th hit of the playoffs. That's one shy of tying Rocchio (11 in 2024) for the most hits by a Cleveland rookie in a single postseason. Rocchio went 1-for-3 on Saturday and is 4-for-28 through nine postseason games.
Anything else fans might want to know?
• Bazzana recorded his first career postseason home run with a solo shot in the 7th inning on Saturday, becoming the first Australian-born player to homer in MLB postseason history.
• Ramírez walked in the sixth inning to extend his postseason on-base streak to 16 games, which ties Steven Kwan (Oct. 8, 2022-Oct. 19, 2024) for the longest in Cleveland postseason history.
• Mesa recorded his second outfield assist of the postseason in Game 4, throwing out DeLauter at second base in the 1st inning. He’s the fourth player in Rays postseason history with multiple outfield assists, joining B.J. Upton, Kevin Kiermaier and Hunter Renfroe (each had two outfield assists for the Rays).

item.content:encoded:
The wildest weekend of the college football season was nonstop drama from the noon slate all the way through to the final snap of the night out West, so naturally that had a massive impact on the way the postseason looks. As much focus as there is on the expansion to the College Football Playoff, this year there are still only 12 teams and the at-large spots are getting tight given the number of potential 10–2/9–3 teams in the Big 12, Big Ten and SEC.
That’s reflected in the Sports Illustrated latest bowl projections going into Week 8, which sees some fascinating CFP matchups from the first round (Texas Tech’s Joey McGuire gets his much-anticipated game against Notre Dame) all the way through to a rematch of last year’s title game in Las Vegas. The rest of the postseason is full of equally fun games, from the possibility of Bill Belichick getting drenched in mayo against Penn State, another West Coast meeting between USC and Texas (in Vegas), an old Big Eight reunion in the Liberty Bowl and a heck of a FBS caper for North Dakota State against a fellow Group of 6 power in the desert.

item.title: [fansided.com] Ranking Tarik Skubal suitors from favorites to dark horses
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. item.content:encoded:
Tarik Skubal and the Los Angeles Dodgers were swept out of the NLCS by the 103-win Milwaukee Brewers, a refreshing change of pace after two years of Dodgers dominance — and a helpful reminder to the MLB owners that payroll alone does not determine winning. It also leaves Skubal with a more difficult decision in free agency than many expected.
The Dodgers will not re-sign Skubal before the lockout in December, as there's simply too much risk without knowing how the salary cap will function come 2027. Really regardless of how MLB's labor dispute plays out, however, Los Angeles will hope to retain Skubal, who is still rightly regarded as the most bankable ace in baseball. The question is: Are the Dodgers the favorites for his services? Let's rank all realistic suitors, from least to most realistic.
8. Philadelphia Phillies
The Phillies are desperate and the Phillies typically spend money. Not necessarily as liberally as fans would like, but it's not impossible to imagine Dave Dombrowski — with the World Series window closing rapidly on this aging core — deciding that Skubal is worth an all-in push.
It would give Philadelphia the most talented rotation in MLB between Skubal, Zack Wheeler, Cristopher Sánchez, Jesús Luzardo and Aaron Nola, four of whom could compete for NL Cy Young next season. There's also Andrew Painter, a former top prospect who came into his own down the stretch and delivered big outs in the postseason, to provide depth.
The Phillies probably have enough money wrapped up in that rotation (and in Bryce Harper, Kyle Schwarber and Trea Turner) to be turned off of paying Skubal top dollar, but it's a fun thought for a team hoping to lean even more on run prevention moving forward.
7. Boston Red Sox
The Red Sox wielded one of the deepest and most reliable rotations in MLB last season; that was with top ace Garrett Crochet on the IL. Upon Crochet's return, Boston will have a compelling blend of experience (Crochet, Ranger Suárez) and emerging youth (Payton Tolle, Jake Bennett) to throw at their opponents.
Then again, they know the toll injuries can take, and Sonny Gray — probably their best regular season starter this past season — is now a free agent. The Red Sox could simply line up a new contract for Gray and be content, but why not aim higher? Skubal has proven remarkably durable over the years and he offers Boston a much longer window as Crochet's partner in crime. Suddenly, the Red Sox have the best one-two punch in baseball and it wouldn't be especially close.
After the Yankees lit them up in the Wild Card round (and after Boston's top arms couldn't pitch deep into either postseason game), there's pressure for a big swing.
6. Chicago Cubs
There's no doubting the Cubs' ability to generate offense, but the rotation has been a sore spot for years now. Jed Hoyer has shown a great appetite for spending in free agency of late; the Alex Bregman signing was a real flex. That said, Chicago needs to allocate more resources toward pitching. The Edward Cabrera trade went belly up. Shōta Imanaga is a free agent now, as are trade deadline pickups Kevin Gausman and Clay Holmes.
Chicago will get help internally with both Cade Horton and Justin Steele returning from season-long elbow injuries; Ben Brown, who finally broke out in 2026, should also be back in the mix. Beyond them, however, it's pretty grim. Matthew Boyd and Javier Assad can eat innings in the regular season, but neither has proven able to pitch deep in October — at least not consistently.
Skubal would deliver Chicago the frontline ace it has long lacked, with a solid scaffolding of talent behind him. The Cubs would be much better positioned to challenge Milwaukee in the division and potentially emerge from a crowded National League field.
5. Detroit Tigers
Skubal has made it clear he would've spent his entire career in Detroit if it was up to him. All the Tigers need to do is come through with a competitive offer. While last year's surprise Framber Valdez signing was a positive indication of the front office's competitive intent, there's a reason no Skubal extension ever came to fruition — or even remotely close.
A client of Scott Boras, Skubal was never inclined to sign an extension. But the Tigers' offers weren't even in the parking lot, much less the ballpark. Detroit will need to scale up its ambition significantly if it wants to lure Skubal back to the midwest.
All that said, Skubal has an affection for Detroit that's worth mentioning. The Tigers also desperately need a frontline ace in Skubal's mold. Young bucks like Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe and River Ryan are very talented, but the Tigers don't really have an established vet besides Valdez, who was a mess last season.
4. New York Yankees
The Yankees tend to flex their muscles in free agency, although with diminishing returns in recent years. New York is no longer the most lucrative destination for a lot of A-tier stars. Juan Soto a couple years ago, Kyle Tucker last winter; the Yankees are getting outbid pretty consistently these days. That has not stopped New York from stockpiling stars, though, especially in the rotation.
It would require Hal Steinbrenner and the front office to basically sign off on a blank check, but the Yankees' ALDS loss to the Rays was a sobering defeat. There are cracks in the foundation. Many of those cracks are injury-related and concentrated in the lineup; Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodón is as strong a four-man gauntlet as any rotation in MLB. The Yankees also have Ryan Weathers, Will Warren and top prospects like Elmer Rodríguez and Carlos Lagrange for depth.
Still, the Yankees know the importance of depth, especially as their non-Schlittler core ages and becomes more injury-prone. Skubal provides stability and instantly lends credibility to any postseason aspirations. Schlittler-Skubal becomes the most fearsome pitching duo in baseball. Never say never.
3. Toronto Blue Jays
The Blue Jays have steadily become the most aggressive front office in the American League. After finishing runner-up in the Juan Soto and Shohei Ohtani sweepstakes, Toronto extended Vladimir Guerrero Jr. at a $500 million price point and signed Dylan Cease in the early days of free agency last winter. A disappointing season should not preclude Toronto from maintaining its all-in approach; if anything, it's more motivation for the Blue Jays to stack talent. This team was in the World Series a year ago.
Toronto is a great market, with a vibrant local culture and an entire country behind the Blue Jays. That ought to appeal to the vanity of a star like Skubal, who would team up with the projected AL Cy Young runner-up in Cease. The Jays also made a savvy trade for José Soriano at the deadline, adding another premium arm in his prime. Trey Yesavage, once healthy, could resume his ascent to stardom. The talent is there.
Skubal solidifies Toronto as a legitimate World Series contender coming into 2027. Moreover, the Jays have a lot of money coming off the books, which should free up the front office to spend recklessly where it counts. Toronto is always the "dark horse" in these top-dollar bidding wars, but ruling out the Blue Jays would be foolish.
2. Los Angeles Dodgers
It's impossible to rule out the incumbents. Los Angeles made the Skubal trade in part because of their deep farm system — and in part because it set the stage for a potential long-term partnership. There's a reason small-market front offices were unwilling to match L.A.'s outgoing package (see: Brewers). The Dodgers could afford to trade two of the 50ish best prospects in baseball because the team can feel reasonably good about both competing for a World Series this season (oh well) and re-signing Skubal when he hits the open market.
An NLCS loss does complicate the situation somewhat, not to mention the unknowability of upcoming labor disputes. The Dodgers' loss was a direct result of investing hundreds of millions of dollars in stars who are beginning to decline. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Shohei Ohtani, Will Smith, Tyler Glasnow and Blake Snell are all on the wrong side of 30; Tucker will join that list next season. Los Angeles will endure more and more diminishing returns.
That said, nothing (besides a strict salary cap) can really stop the Dodgers from compensating for declining stars by signing more expensive stars, even if it leaves the cap sheet in utter chaos five years from now. That has been L.A.'s strategy to date; it was part of the logic behind the Skubal trade. The Dodgers still arguably represent Skubal's best chance to win a World Series, which will no doubt be part of the calculus if another team can't dramatically outspend them.
1. New York Mets
If any team can blow L.A.'s offer out of the water, it's the Mets. Steve Cohen is baseball's richest owner and New York has consistently tossed its hat in the ring for MLB's premium free agents. Juan Soto's $765 million contract set a new record; Skubal very well could set a record for pitchers.
The Mets are coming off of a last-place season, too, which only fuels anxiety in the fan base. It should also fuel aggression in the front office. David Stearns is under pressure to prove that he has what it takes to win in New York. Skubal would join an emerging ace in Nolan McLean, plus other whippersnappers like Zac Thornton and Jonah Tong. The Mets need depth besides, as Kodai Senga and Sean Manaea look more like bullpen arms these days. New York, however, is the one non-Dodgers team with enough money to sign Skubal and pursue other targets.
If the Dodgers get spooked by the shadow of their own payroll, which is more likely than ever, the Mets are the logical team we can expect to swoop in and win the Skubal bidding war outright.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Back-and-Forth ALCS Could Spell Trouble for Brewers in World Series
item.dc:creator: Curt Bishop
item.description: The Milwaukee Brewers made quick work of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first trip to the World Series in 44 years. Now, the Brewers are awaiting the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays, which is tied at two games apiece heading into Sunday's Game 5. The series will go at least six games at this point, which means whoever wins it will only have a few days off before the series beg
item.content:encoded:
The Milwaukee Brewers made quick work of the Los Angeles Dodgers in the National League Championship Series to secure their first trip to the World Series in 44 years. Now, the Brewers are awaiting the winner of the American League Championship Series between the Cleveland Guardians and Tampa Bay Rays, which is tied at two games apiece heading into Sunday's Game 5.
The series will go at least six games at this point, which means whoever wins it will only have a few days off before the series begins. This could ultimately spell some trouble for the Brewers, who have a ton of extra rest.
How extra rest can affect teams
Extra rest can help. The Washington Nationals had a week over before the 2019 World Series while the Houston Astros only had two days. Washington proceeded to win the first two games on the road and ultimately win the series in seven games.
However, there have been plenty of cases in which extra rest hasn't exactly been kind to teams. The Detroit Tigers had a week off before the 2006 World Series, while the St. Louis Cardinals won the NLCS in seven games and only had one day. St. Louis made quick work of the Tigers, winning in five games.
The same thing happened to Detroit in 2012 when they swept the ALCS and waited around for the San Francisco Giants to come back from 3-1 to win the series. At that point, the Giants had the momentum and ultimately swept the Tigers.
The 2007 Colorado Rockies and 2015 New York Mets also had extra rest before the World Series and were eliminated quickly. So, it can certainly hurt at times.
Perhaps it could ultimately help the Brewers instead. There's really no way of knowing for sure, as it can work both ways. But things will get interesting if the ALCS goes the full seven games. The winner of that series would only have two days off before the series while Milwaukee will have had over a week.
A case could be made that it just gives the Brewers more time to prepare, and that is certainly true. But teams can also lose their edge when they aren't playing for a week or more before the World Series, so it will be very interesting to see just how it affects the Brewers as they prepare for their first World Series since 1982.
Curt Bishop is a freelance sports writer who graduated from Maryville University of St. Louis with a Bachelor of Arts degree in the field of Communication and currently writes as a contributor for various platforms covering Major League Baseball. Curt’s work includes covering trade and free agency predictions, as well as rumors and news. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Milwaukee Brewers On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

He goes only if he wants to go. Harper had repeatedly said that But if the Phillies are seeking real change this offseason, every potential move has to be on the table. item.content:encoded:
Will the Phillies trade Bryce Harper this offseason? It’s very unlikely. Harper, one of only two well above average hitters for the Phillies in 2026, has a full no-trade clause. He goes only if he wants to go. Harper had repeatedly said that
But if the Phillies are seeking real change this offseason, every potential move has to be on the table.
Should the Phillies keep Harper heading into year nine of his 13-year contract or should Dave Dombrowski make a seismic trade and move on from “The Showman?”
Here’s part two of Phillies Nation’s Stay or Go series. Vote in our poll below the article.
Past editions:
Destiny Lugardo — Site Director: Stay
Flipping Harper for multiple lineup pieces would represent dramatic change, but Harper has a full-no trade clause and is committed to Philly for the next five years. If he leaves, it’s because he wants to go elsewhere. I’m not a mind reader, but I don’t think Harper is quite there yet. It could happen eventually, but not now.
Ty Daubert — Editorial Director: Stay
According to OPS+, the Phillies had two regulars who produced at an above-average offensive clip in 2026: Kyle Schwarber (128) and Harper (131). Philadelphia needs more capable, effective hitters, and Harper was its best this season. The team could probably use some shaking up after another early exit, but moving on from Harper would only make the underwhelming lineup harder to bulk up. If anything, his productive 162-game, 107-walk year should give the Phillies a bit of additional confidence in his abilities as he heads into his age-34 season.
Bailey Digh — Staff Writer: Stay
The Phillies are going to try to win in 2027. Harper will help with that. He remains one of baseball’s best hitters. He was one of the few things that did not go wrong for the Phillies this year. There’s so much to do this offseason for this club, and there’s going to be a lockout. This offseason isn’t one to make a major move like trading Harper, an idea that only gets thrown out there from people who don’t work for the Phillies.
Nathan Ackerman — Staff Writer: Stay
The Phillies this offseason are going to need to make changes, while resisting the idea of making changes for the sake of making changes if they can’t execute the right changes. Any attempt to move Harper would qualify as that. A team whose offense is arguably its weakest unit – that’s saying something, given the bullpen, which should be much easier to remake – should not try to jettison the player who posted their highest regular-season OPS while playing in all 162 games, before producing in the short postseason. And as bad as the on-field impact would be, the organizational optics would perhaps be just as bad.

item.content:encoded:
Game 5 of the ALCS between the Tampa Bay Rays and Cleveland Guardians takes place on Sunday afternoon, and these teams are knotted at two games apiece after Tampa Bay won Game 4.
There are a ton of props to consider in Game 5 of the ALCS, including a home run prop or two as these teams look to deliver a key blow before the series shifts back to Tampa Bay on Monday.
Drew Rasmussen (14 home runs allowed in the regular season, two in the postseason) and Parker Messick (17 home runs allowed in the regular season, one in the postseason) are on the mound in this game.
The total (6.5) is pretty low in this matchup, so we may not see a ton of offense.
While betting on home runs is a fun way to get involved in the action, these props are extremely tough to hit with the pitching in the postseason. Still, there have been a few long balls in this series, and I’m targeting one player that has already gone deep over the course of the first four games to stay hot on Sunday.
Best MLB Home Run Prop Bet Picks for ALCS Game 5
Chase DeLauter to Hit a Home Run (+970)
Chase DeLauter homered 16 times during the regular season, and he took Drew Rasmussen deep in Game 1.
The Guardians youngster was 1-for-3 against the Rays ace in the series opener, and he’s 2-for-4 against him in the regular season in his career.
DeLauter is dangerous against right-handed pitching, homering 13 times while posting an .808 OPS during the regular season.
He’s also been hot in this series, picking up five hits, three RBIs and three runs scored in four games. Overall, he’s hitting .294 with two doubles in a homer in the 2026 postseason.
There are worse bets to make at nearly 10/1 odds in Game 5.
Junior Caminero to Hit a Home Run (+497)
During the regular season, Junior Caminero hit 42 home runs and was elite against left-handed pitching.
He had a .287 batting average, a .916 OPS and homered eight times against southpaws. He has not had a ton of success against Messick in his career (1-for-12), but the lefty did allow 17 home runs in the 2026 regular season.
At some point, Caminero is going to get a hold of a ball, as he’s yet to go deep in the playoffs. Still, Caminero is hitting, picking up at least one hit in three games in this series, including two doubles.
This prop has skyrocketed all the way to +497 with Messick on the mound, but the Guardians’ bullpen has been taxed over the last few days and could be vulnerable to a long ball.
With just one game to bet on, I’m going to take a shot on the best power hitter for either team to leave the yard on Sunday.
Odds refresh periodically and are subject to change.

Peter is the associate managing editor for Sports Illustrated Betting. He has worked as a writer and editor for BetSided, NBC Sports, the Connecticut Sun and the Meriden Record-Journal covering the NBA, WNBA, NFL, MLB, betting and more. item.title: [FanSided] Projecting MLB free agency deals for Tarik Skubal and baseball's biggest stars
item.dc:creator: Christopher Kline
item.description: MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point. What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according t
item.content:encoded:
MLB free agency takes on a new urgency this winter with a Dec. 1 lockout on the horizon. That could change how teams operate — and, eventually, how much money teams are allowed to spend, or even forced to spend. There are a ton of unknown variables at this point.
What we do know (for the most part) are which stars will be available to sign when the market does open up. From Los Angeles Dodgers ace Tarik Skubal to top Japanese free agent Teruaki Sato, here are the 10 best free agents (according to FanSided's Robert Murray) with projected contracts and destinations.
LHP Tarik Skubal
Projected deal: 9 years, $378 million ($42 million AAV) with New York Mets
Regardless of how CBA negotiations shake out, Tarik Skubal's long-rumored $400 million price tag may ultimately prove to be an overestimation. There's a reason no pitcher has ever received such a paycheck, Shohei Ohtani notwithstanding. Still, Skubal should become the highest-paid pitcher in MLB history. His durability, both in-game and season-long, combined with razor-sharp stuff in the prime of his career, should give teams the confidence to invest in Skubal over an extended period.
The Dodgers are the natural landing spot after acquiring him at the trade deadline, but the Mets are baseball's richest team and there's mounting pressure for New York to start competing, in a serious way, with Juan Soto and Francisco Lindor. Skubal is the ultimate floor-raiser in a rotation, and he'd form a mean one-two punch with breakout ace Nolan McLean.
OF Seiya Suzuki
Projected deal: 4 years, $100 million ($25 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Seiya Suzuki is probably the best bat available in free agency. The 32-year-old outfielder has been a model of consistency for the Cubs, with at least 20 home runs and an .800-plus OPS in three straight seasons. He's a plus defender in right field, too, where he posted career-best metrics in 2026. Suzuki has a rocket-like arm and consistently holds runners from the back corner.
Plenty of teams will take an interest in Suzuki's right-handed power profile; he draws walks and operates with sage discipline in the batter's box, despite occasionally elevated strikeout numbers. In the end, Toronto represents the most logical intersection of need and financial firepower to outbid the field.
OF Randy Arozarena
Projected deal: 5 years, $110 million ($22 million AAV) with Philadelphia Phillies
Randy Arozarena set new career highs in average (.281), OPS (.865) and home runs (26) in his walk year, emerging as one of the few bright spots on an otherwise disappointing Mariners team. He's more adequate than exceptional with his glove, but Arozarena provides middle-order power and he's a great personality hire.
The Phillies need Arozarena's bat and competitive fire in equal measure, plus he can help to safely return Bryce Harper to first base next season. Philadelphia desperately needs a right-handed slugger behind Harper in the lineup; the ability to finally add some stability to the outfield depth chart, as opposed to a 2026 rewind of the Adolis García or Max Kepler situations, should greatly appeal to a desperate Dave Dombrowski.
3B Teruaki Sato
Projected deal: 3 years, $75 million ($25 million AAV) with New York Yankees
Teruaki Sato is the most accomplished international free agent hoping to come Stateside this offseason. An MVP candidate in Japan's NPB, Sato hit .306 this year with 39 home runs and a .991 OPS. There are swing-and-miss and defense concerns, not dissimilar to the vague uncertainties that tanked Munetaka Murakami's stock last winter. Murakami ended up on a two-year deal with the White Sox, which he immediately outperformed.
Sato's left-handed power and upside at 27 years old could mean his market flourishes. But, given the baked-in gambles that come with signing an international free agent, he could end up getting lowballed, much like Murakami. A three-year, $75 million contract gives Sato a nice payday upfront while still hedging against potential struggles with a short-term framework. The Yankees need an infield slugger and have the money to roll the dice, so to speak, on Sato's immense talent.
LHP Trevor Rogers
Projected deal: 3 years, $60 million ($20 million) with Baltimore Orioles
Trevor Rogers has dealt with his share of injuries and inconsistency over the years, but he's coming off of two strong campaigns in Baltimore — and he's only 28 years old, so there's room left to establish himself as more than a third or fourth starter type. He couldn't recapture the success of 2025, when Rogers returned from injury to post a 1.81 ERA in 18 starts, but his 4.03 ERA last season does not capture the strength of his stuff (3.60 xERA). Moreover, the career-high 30 starts and 169.2 innings pitched was a nice addition to his résumé.
Teams will probably balk at dropping a full bag on Rogers' doorstep, ultimately, which opens the door for a short-term contract (probably with an opt-out clause or two) and a return to Baltimore. The Orioles need pitching badly and there are precious few better options than Rogers floating around the open market. This contract could turn into a total bargain.
RHP Freddy Peralta
Projected deal: 4 years, $84 million ($21 million AAV) with Chicago Cubs
Freddy Peralta's walk year has been a roller coaster of emotions. He bombed in New York after the Mets dealt multiple top-100 prospects to acquire him in an offseason trade. Then, after relocating to Tampa at the trade deadline, Peralta started slow before gradually picking up steam in September. Down the stretch and into the playoffs, he has looked more like the Cy Young candidate we witnessed in Milwaukee last season.
Peralta has not made the strongest case to prospective suitors in 2026, so a one-year, high-AAV deal to "prove it" is on the table. Ultimately, however, the 30-year-old should still be able to coax a substantial multi-year offer out of a desperate contender. His longtime NL Central rivals, the Cubs, are one such desperate contender. Peralta could join with the now-healthy Cade Horton and Justin Steele to revitalize Chicago's World Series hopes for 2027.
C Ryan Jeffers
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Minnesota Twins
The catcher market is tough to project, as there are so few who can hit like Ryan Jeffers. He was excellent in Minnesota this season, with 14 home runs and an .814 OPS in roughly half a season. He's the best catcher on the market, but Jeffers is not exactly lauded for his defense nor his game management behind the plate. He is not without injury concerns either, while even the best catchers end up in a timeshare eventually (especially when, like Jeffers, their glovework can be problematic).
Since there is such an absence of reliable hitters at the catcher position, Jeffers should be able to land a solid multi-year deal in the middle of his prime. A return to the Twins should not be discounted, even with Eduardo Tait and Vahn Lackey coming up through the Minors on accelerated timelines. Minnesota made a conscious decision not to trade him at the deadline, after all. The Twins would probably like to compete next season.
RHP Michael King
Projected deal: five years, $120 million ($24 million AAV) with San Diego Padres
Michael King returned to San Diego last winter on a backloaded three-year deal with opt outs. After an excellent showing in the playoffs, he will probably axe the remaining two years and $66 million on that contract in hopes of securing more guaranteed money this winter. King is not the sexiest name on the pitching market by any stretch, but he has made himself into a dependable workhorse with October equity.
The Padres clearly love King and new ownership, with their stated intention to build a contender, will probably consent to a reworked contract. San Diego has a paper-thin rotation as is. Losing King without a viable alternative in place could be disastrous, as the Padres don't have the trade ammo to compensate for a free agency exodus.
2B Brandon Lowe
Projected deal: 3 years, $66 million ($22 million AAV) with Pittsburgh Pirates
Brandon Lowe arrived in Pittsburgh via offseason trade and immediately became the most bankable presence in their lineup, with 35 home runs, 96 RBI and an .824 OPS. The 32-year-old can get in trouble with swing-and-miss, but he's a slugging outlier at second base. Moreover, Lowe quietly posted some of the best defensive metrics in MLB last season after struggling for years on the defensive end. It's fair to be skeptical about Lowe's ability to sustain this elite defense into his mid-30s, but he did everything he could to maximize his value as a free agent.
To that point, it's hard to imagine the Pirates letting Lowe walk without a fight. Pittsburgh threw more money around last offseason, with the front office clearly committed to changing their postseason fortunes. It did not come together in 2026, but Pittsburgh has a dangerous lineup and a very talented pitching staff. There's potential for a breakthrough in 2027, especially if Lowe sticks around.
LHP Adrián Morejón
Projected deal: 4 years, $68 million ($17 million AAV) with Toronto Blue Jays
Adrián Morejón's mystery-shrouded absence in San Diego's NLDS loss to Milwaukee was a tough pill to swallow, but once again, the Padres end the season feeling like the second-best team in the National League. They were able to at least put a scare into the Brewers where even the Dodgers could not. Part of the reason for San Diego's success this season, despite dramatic fluctuations from their lineup, was an elite bullpen. Morejón was only the setup man to Mason Miller, but the 27-year-old southpaw is still among the best relievers in baseball.
Over the past three seasons, Morejón has a 2.58 ERA with 248 strikeouts in 223.1 innings. It's hard to find a more steadfast high-leverage arm, especially one as young as Morejón. He could get some real length on his contract in a reliever-needy marketplace. The Blue Jays figure to be as aggressive as any team this offseason; Morejón setting up Louis Varland, with Tyler Rogers and Spencer Miles to cover other late-inning spots, is a tantalizing proposition.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Kyle Tucker sends promising message to Dodgers fans after atrocious debut season
item.dc:creator: Valentina Martinez
item.description: The Dodgers face several questions after an early postseason exit in the National League Championship Series. The dynasty that the Dodgers have put together is in jeopardy of ending within the next few seasons if the front office can't assemble another winning roster. Kyle Tucker, who was signed to a four-year, $240 million deal ahead of the 2026 season, addressed fans as the future of the franchise is in limbo. "Through every high and low, thank you to our fans for riding with us all season. We
item.content:encoded:
The Dodgers face several questions after an early postseason exit in the National League Championship Series.
The dynasty that the Dodgers have put together is in jeopardy of ending within the next few seasons if the front office can't assemble another winning roster. Kyle Tucker, who was signed to a four-year, $240 million deal ahead of the 2026 season, addressed fans as the future of the franchise is in limbo.
"Through every high and low, thank you to our fans for riding with us all season. We appreciate the love and support more than you know. This isn't the end — we'll be back," Tucker wrote in an Instagram post.
For most of 2026, the four-time All-Star was far from full form. Tucker ended the regular season with a .233 batting average, 17 home runs and 70 RBIs. He entered October with a .715 OPS, the lowest mark since his debut season in 2018 when he played 28 games.
Tucker's struggles became a point of contention among the fan base, but the star outfielder came to life in the postseason. The 29-year-old averaged .333 with a .967 OPS in October, which was perhaps the only highlight of his inaugural Dodgers season.
The Dodgers, who face an uncertain future after the failed quest for a three-peat, will need Tucker to play at All-Star strength the entire 2027 season as one of the many veterans on the roster. While Tucker's performance next year can't be known, one thing is certain, the Dodgers will surely try to get younger this winter.

item.content:encoded:
Earlier this week, White Sox GM Chris Getz spoke to the media for the first time since Chicago’s ALDS Game 5 loss against the Guardians. Getz reflected on the season and provided some updates on the future. Among the topics of conversation were positions the White Sox will pursue upgrades in during the upcoming offseason, with Getz emphasizing the starting rotation as an obvious area of need. I previously discussed a few starting pitching options I’d like to see the White Sox pursue, so this will be a bit of a different conversation. Let’s discuss a dream target, a realistic target, and a mistake the White Sox could make in their pitching search.
Dream Target: LHP Tarik Skubal
It’s impossible to discuss the pitching free agent class without mentioning two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal, the best pitcher available by a wide margin and one of the most dominant arms in all of baseball. The soon-to-be 30-year-old spent the first six and a half seasons with the Tigers before a midseason trade sent him to the Dodgers. He won the Cy Young Award in both 2024 and 2025, with a 2.39 and 2.21 ERA in each year, and would’ve been squarely in the mix for 2026 as well if not for an injury that cost him six weeks in May and June.
Do I think the White Sox have any chance at landing Tarik Skubal? Probably not. To be honest, I’d be surprised if they’re even interested. But Chicago has a very low payroll and an obvious need in the starting rotation. In theory, they could add Skubal for $30-40 million a year and still have payroll room for other upgrades on the roster. They’re a young, exciting team who seems to be just beginning their competitive window, so it’s a destination that could be appealing for Skubal. He’ll no doubt have his pick though, and it’s hard to see the White Sox competing financially with some of the other markets. I guess one can dream.
Realistic Target: RHP Tyler Mahle
Maybe big-game hunting isn’t realistic for the White Sox this offseason, but there’s no reason they can’t add at least one impact starting pitcher in free agency. Braves righty Tyler Mahle is an interesting veteran arm who shined during the second half of the season and into the playoffs. While most pitchers traded at the deadline struggled in their new home, Mahle posted a 1.99 ERA in nine starts with Atlanta and allowed just two earned runs in 13.1 innings in the Postseason. Mahle turned 32 in September and will be looking to leverage his strong finish into a solid contract. Perhaps a two or three-year deal could be in the cards for a player who’s always had a productive career but has battled frequent injuries. Mahle would be a strong veteran presence in the White Sox rotation and has a recent history of Postseason success. He could be one of the names on Chicago’s target list.
Mistake: LHP Robbie Ray
Left-hander Robbie Ray was one of the most talked about names ahead of the trade deadline, and the Giants ultimately dealt him within their division to the San Diego Padres. Some concerning metrics made Ray a prime candidate for regression, and he posted just a 5.02 ERA in nine starts for San Diego down the stretch. Still, he has back to back seasons with an ERA under 3.70, so he’s deserving of a big league deal this offseason. I don’t think that should be the White Sox, however. Ray is now 35 years old and his underlying metrics were scary in 2026. He pitched in two ballparks that heavily favor pitchers, whereas Chicago is a more hitter-friendly environment. Ray is a veteran who has struggled in the playoffs in his career, and his age is a real concern. I’d stay away here if I were the White Sox.

item.title: [fansided.com] The stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal, with one giant asterisk standing in their way
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: The offseason is a perfect time for New York Mets fans like myself to be optimistic, and that's exactly what I'm going to be doing here when I say the stars are aligning for the Mets to sign Tarik Skubal in free agency. I know, this seems crazy. Why would Skubal want to join a Mets team that just won 74 games in 2026 and has failed to make the playoffs in each of Juan Soto's two years in Flushing?
